# Frame Job User Guide

Frame Job is a native macOS video editor for Apple Silicon Macs running
macOS 26 or later. You open a movie, arrange it on layered tracks over a fixed
canvas, then trim, cut, grade, caption, animate and export it. Every edit you
make in the window can also be made by an AI agent over MCP, or by the built-in
Assistant.

The quickest way in: **File ▸ Open…** (⌘O) on a movie makes an untitled project
sized and timed to it, with the movie on Track 1, ready to cut. Save writes a
`.framejob` package.

## The pages

Read the first four in order to learn the editor; the rest stand alone.

1. [Projects and media](projects-and-media.md) — starting, saving and opening projects, the `.framejob` package, the Document tab's canvas settings, importing files, the Media tab and relinking.
2. [The timeline and playback](timeline.md) — the editor window, tracks and their switches, the ruler and playhead, zoom, selection, snapping, markers, the in/out range and playback.
3. [Editing clips](editing.md) — placing, moving, trimming, slipping, splitting, deleting and closing gaps, copy and paste, and nests.
4. [Canvas, layers, text and shapes](canvas-and-layers.md) — placing a picture on the canvas, opacity, blend modes, shadows and filters, text, shape, image and background clips, and matte tracks.
5. [Motion, actions and transitions](motion-and-transitions.md) — actions that animate a clip's properties over time, motion presets, and transitions between clips.
6. [Speed, reverse and freeze frames](speed.md) — constant speed, fitting a clip to a length, rate stretch, speed ramps and their presets, reversing and freeze frames.
7. [Audio](audio.md) — clip levels, fades and their shapes, ducking by clip length or by speech, noise reduction, compression, pan, mute and solo, Normalize and Synchronize Audio.
8. [Remove Silences and Remove Filler Words](cleanup-tools.md) — cutting dead air and filler words out of a spoken recording in one step.
9. [Captions and transcription](captions.md) — importing and exporting captions, and transcribing speech on this Mac or with AssemblyAI into subtitles or word-by-word captions.
10. [Colour grading](color-grading.md) — the Color tab, wheels, curves, looks and LUTs, adjustment clips and qualifiers, Show Ungraded and the scopes.
11. [HDR and colour management](hdr-and-color.md) — how sources are read, camera log, SDR and HDR (HLG) projects, blending, and HDR and SDR deliverables.
12. [Motion graphics](graphics.md) — graphic clips, the built-in graphics, their properties in the inspector, and bringing in your own.
13. [Screen recording](screen-recording.md) — recording a display or a window with system audio, microphone and click rings, recording a camera on its own or beside the screen, and recording voice-overs.
14. [Exporting](export.md) — the export sheet, its formats and settings, presets, the Export Queue, and saving single frames.
15. [The Assistant](assistant.md) — chatting with Claude in the inspector to edit the open project, on your own Anthropic key.
16. [Driving Frame Job from an AI agent (MCP)](mcp.md) — connecting an MCP client such as Claude Code, how calls behave, and every tool.
17. [Settings](settings.md) — the Settings window, updates (Check for Updates… in the downloaded copy), the View choices Frame Job remembers, and where it keeps its files.
18. [Menus and keyboard shortcuts](menus-and-shortcuts.md) — every menu command with its shortcut, and the keys, gestures and context menus that have no menu item.

Writing your own graphic module is covered by the
[graphics API reference](../graphics-api.md).

#####
# 1. What this is

A screencast editor without a recorder — and, since road map 3,
a recorder of the SCREEN, and since §11 CAM-1 of a camera beside it or on its
own, whose output is ordinary media. Open one or
more video files from disk, arrange them on layered tracks over a fixed canvas, trim,
split, annotate, animate, and export. Mac only, Apple Silicon, macOS 26+.

The bar is a balance: enough to make a real cut with text,
shapes, transitions and simple animation, without Final Cut's magnetic
timeline, roles, multicam, scopes, or a plugin ecosystem.

Deliberate non-goals: multicam, color grading beyond
per-clip controls (§11 GR-1: tier 1 of grading — tone, adjustment clips,
looks, LUT import, an ungraded switch and one luma waveform — is in, kept by
the owner's verdict of 2026-10-10, and tier 2's scopes, colour wheels,
curves and qualifiers beside it, GR-10…GR-13; tier 3's HDR→SDR conversion
and camera log are in, GR-15, GR-16; the HDR road map's HLG timeline, its
HLG, HDR10 and SDR-version deliverables, HDR scopes, the PQ peak, Canon Log
2 and 3 and opt-in linear-light blending are in, HD-1…HD-17; a wide-gamut
working space for SDR projects is not wanted, GR-20; tier 4's vectorscope zoom,
hue curves, the blend between curves of different point counts and the
qualifier's cleanup blur are in, GR-24, GR-31…GR-35, while an Offset
wheel, a qualifier on picture clips, 1,024-level scopes and a histogram
behind the curves are not wanted, GR-27…GR-30), a plugin system (a clip may
draw itself from a JavaScript module in its package, road map 10; nothing
else is scriptable — §11 G-1),
motion blur, stabilisation, optical-flow retiming and auto-reframe (heavy
pixel work or ML, outside the compositor's one-pass shape — road map 2 §4),
any platform but macOS. **Screen recording was on this list until road map 3
reversed it** (§11): the app records a display or a window through
ScreenCaptureKit into a file it then imports exactly as File ▸ Open would —
paused and resumed from the menu bar, each stretch its own file and its own
clip; callouts reconstructed after the fact stay out. **Camera recording
was on it too until §11 CAM-1** (road map "camera-recording") reversed it: a
camera alone or beside a screen recording, each its own file and clip.
**Audio beyond what shipped was on it too until §11 AU-2** (road map
"audio", 2026-10-30) lifted it: EQ, track and bus processing, and Apple's
built-in audio units are in, beside Frame Job's own DSP; hosting
third-party Audio Unit plug-ins stays out, under the plugin system above.

**The opening flow is the point.** File > Open on a `.mov` or `.mp4` (or a
drop on the Dock icon, or the welcome window's Open Video…) creates an
*untitled* project sized to that file, with the file as the first clip on
Track 1, ready to cut. Save then writes a `.framejob` package next to the
source. The app is also the Alternate handler for movie, audio and image
types so Open With… works from the Finder.

# Projects and media

A Frame Job project is a `.framejob` package: one file in the Finder that holds the edit, the caches that make it quick to reopen, and, when you ask for it, copies of the footage itself. This page covers starting a project (most often by opening a movie), saving it, what is inside the package, the canvas settings on the Document tab, bringing files in, the Media tab, and what to do when files go missing.

## Starting a project

### Open a movie

The quickest way in is to open the footage itself. **File ▸ Open…** (⌘O) on a movie, **Open With ▸ Frame Job** in the Finder (or a double-click, once Frame Job is that file type's default app), a drop on the Dock icon, or a drop onto a Frame Job window all do the same thing:

- an **untitled** project is created, sized and rated to the file;
- the file becomes the first media item and the first clip on Track 1, starting at 0;
- the window is titled after the movie (`Interview.mov` opens as "Interview").

The canvas takes the movie's *display* size, so a portrait phone clip opens as 1080 × 1920, not sideways. Its frame rate is read exactly: a 29.97 or 23.976 file stays 29.97 or 23.976, not 30 or 24.

Opening a sound file works the same way, but a sound file has no picture: its project is 1920 × 1080 at 30 fps. Opening a picture (PNG, JPEG, HEIC) makes a project at the picture's pixel size, 30 fps, with the picture as a 5-second clip.

The new project lives only in memory until you save it, so it opens already marked as changed. Closing it asks whether to save. The first **Save** offers to put the package next to the source file, under the source's name.

Opening a `.framejob` package opens that project (a double-click on a package always opens it in Frame Job). If it is already open, its window comes forward.

Dropping several files at once on a window, the Welcome window or the Dock icon opens each one as its own untitled project. Only `.framejob` packages and the movie, sound and picture types File ▸ Open… lists are taken; anything else dropped there is ignored. To add files to the project you already have open, drop them on the [Media tab](#the-media-tab) instead.

*Agents:* `open_project` (takes a `path` to a package, movie, sound file or picture; answers `already_open: true` when that file is already open).

### New Project

**File ▸ New Project** (⌘N) opens a blank 1920 × 1080, 30 fps project with no dialog, in a window titled "Untitled Project". Change the size and rate afterwards on the Document tab (see [The Document tab](#the-document-tab-canvas-settings)).

*Agents:* `new_project` (an optional `path` saves it there straight away; without one it stays an untitled draft).

### The Welcome window

When Frame Job starts with nothing to open, and when you click its Dock icon with no window open, it shows the Welcome window. It holds:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Open Video…** | The same open panel as File ▸ Open…. |
| **New Project** | A blank 1920 × 1080, 30 fps project. |
| **New Recording…** | Opens the screen recorder panel; see [Screen recording](screen-recording.md). |
| **Recent** | Up to five recently opened projects, by name; hover for the full path. Hidden when there are none. |

The line at the foot lists the file types it opens: MOV · MP4 · M4V · M4A · MP3 · WAV · AIFF · PNG · JPEG · HEIC. You can also drop a file or a package anywhere on the Welcome window to open it. The window closes itself as soon as a project window comes up.

## Saving, reverting and closing

| Command | Shortcut | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **File ▸ New Project** | ⌘N | A blank 1920 × 1080, 30 fps project. |
| **File ▸ Open…** | ⌘O | Opens a package, or builds an untitled project around a movie, sound file or picture. |
| **File ▸ Open Recent ▸** | | Recently opened projects; **Clear Menu** empties the list. |
| **File ▸ Close** | ⌘W | Closes the window. A project that has been saved writes its changes and closes without asking; an untitled project with changes (an opened movie always counts) asks whether to save first. |
| **File ▸ Save** | ⌘S | Writes the package. An untitled project asks where. |
| **File ▸ Save As…** | ⇧⌘S | Writes the project to a new package. |
| **File ▸ Revert To ▸** | | Goes back to the last saved version, or browses earlier versions of the package. |

Once a project has been saved it autosaves in place, the macOS way: changes are written to the package as you work, and the package is written beside the old one and swapped in, so a crash part-way through a save cannot leave half a package behind. Because of this, macOS adds its standard document commands to the File menu: **Duplicate**, **Rename…**, **Move To…**, **Revert To ▸** (in place of Revert to Saved) and **Share**, and the same Rename and Move To controls appear when you click the window's title. A project only ever saves as a `.framejob` package. Making a movie or a still is a separate step; see [Export](export.md).

*Agents:* `save_project` (a `path` is required the first time and always means Save As), `close_project` (refused when `get_project` reports `unsaved_changes` unless `discard: true`, and refused while a sheet is open), `get_project` (the whole project as JSON plus the playhead, selection, in/out range, `unsaved_changes` and `missing_media`). `new_project` adds `.framejob` to a `path` that lacks it. `new_project` and `save_project` refuse a path another open project holds (close that one first) or one a window is still opening.

## What a `.framejob` package holds

A package is a folder that the Finder shows as one file:

| Inside | What it is |
|---|---|
| `project.json` | The edit itself: canvas, media list, tracks, clips, markers. The only thing a package needs in order to open. |
| `cache/` | Things Frame Job can rebuild: filmstrip thumbnails, waveforms, the voice-detection and sync analyses, transcripts, reversed clips and speed-ramp audio. A package with a missing or damaged `cache/` still opens and just redraws. |
| `media/` | Only after **Consolidate Media…**: copies of the footage (see [Consolidate Media](#consolidate-media)). |
| `graphics/` | Only once you add a graphic: graphic modules, their fonts, images and kept versions. See [Graphics](graphics.md). |

**Media is referenced, not copied.** By default a project remembers where each file lives (its path and a Finder bookmark, so a moved file is often found again) and reads it from there. The package stays small, but it depends on the footage staying put. Consolidate Media is how you make a package hold everything it needs.

Caches are built in the background after an open, an import or a relink, and the timeline fills in as they finish. Frame Job builds at most two files' sound caches at a time, on threads of their own, so importing many long files at once does not hold up playback or a speed ramp's sound. A cache that already matches its file is never rebuilt. Moving, copying or consolidating the package keeps its caches. Until an untitled project is first saved, its caches live in a temporary folder; the first save copies them in.

*Transcripts* cost money to rebuild when they came from the cloud engine, so treat `cache/transcripts/` as worth keeping. See [Captions](captions.md).

## The Document tab: canvas settings

The canvas is the fixed frame every clip is composited into, and every export starts from its size. It is set on the inspector's **Document** tab, in five sections. Every change there to the project is one undo step (**Resize clips proportionally** is a preference on this Mac, not part of the project, so it is not undone).

### Document (summary)

Read-only rows: **Resolution**, **Frame rate**, **Duration**, **Tracks**, **Background** (Black, White, a `#RRGGBB` value, "Transparent", or a colour with its opacity as a percentage) and **Colour** ("SDR — Rec. 709" or "HDR — Rec. 2100 HLG").

### Canvas

| Control | What it does | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Preset** | 1080p · 1920 × 1080, 4K · 3840 × 2160, 720p · 1280 × 720, Vertical · 1080 × 1920, Square · 1080 × 1080, 1440p · 2560 × 1440, or **Source Size** (the size of the first media file that has one). Shows **Custom** when the size matches none of these. | 1080p |
| **Width** / **Height** | Type an even number of pixels from 16 to 16384. | 1920 × 1080 |
| **Resize clips proportionally** | When on, changing the size also scales every clip's position and scale by the same ratio, so the layout looks the same at the new size. When off, clips keep their pixel positions. Remembered on this Mac, not in the project. | Off |
| **Dynamic Range** | SDR or HDR (HLG). See [HDR and colour](hdr-and-color.md). | SDR |
| **Blending** | Encoded or Linear light. See [HDR and colour](hdr-and-color.md). | Encoded |

Choosing **Custom** in the popup only beeps; type the size into Width and Height instead. **Source Size** also beeps when no media file has a picture size.

Width and height must both be even. An odd value is refused, for example "canvas width must be even (h.264 encodes in macroblocks), not 1081". A project opened from an odd-sized movie keeps that size, but once you change either field both sides are checked, and Source Size on an odd-sized file is refused the same way.

### Frame Rate

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Rate** | 24, 23.976, 25, 30, 29.97, 50, 60, or **Match First Clip**, which takes the rate of the earliest clip on the timeline whose file has video (beeps if there is none). |
| **Duration** | Read-only: the timeline's length. |

A project can run at a rate the popup does not list. An opened file at 24, 23.976, 25, 30, 29.97, 48, 50, 60 or 59.94 fps keeps that exact rate; any other rate (screen recordings often have odd ones) is kept to three decimals. The popup then shows **24**, while the Document summary's **Frame rate** row shows the real rate. Picking a popup item changes the rate, and **Match First Clip** brings the file's rate back.

Changing the rate moves every clip start, length, action and marker onto the new frame grid. If two markers land on the same frame at the new rate, the later one is dropped.

### Appearance

| Control | What it does | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Background** | The colour behind every layer. Lower its opacity for a transparent background; the section's note then names the export formats that keep transparency, or counts them when there are three or more. | Black, opaque |
| **Timecode** | Frames (`HH:MM:SS:FF`) or Milliseconds (`HH:MM:SS.mmm`), everywhere the project shows a time. | Frames |
| **Fit new clips to canvas** | A clip added from a file larger than the canvas is scaled down to fit. | On |

**Reset** on the section header puts all three back to their defaults. It is offered only while one of them differs.

### Markers

Every marker in the project, with its name, **Chapter**, **Go** and **Delete**. See [Timeline](timeline.md).

*Agents:* `set_canvas` (takes `width`, `height`, `fps`, `background`, `rescale_clips`, `fit_new_clips`, `timecode_frames`, `output`, `blending`; anything left out keeps its value; `fps` takes any `[num, den]`).

## Bringing files in

### What Frame Job reads

| Kind | Files |
|---|---|
| Movies | MOV, MP4, M4V and other containers macOS plays: H.264, HEVC, ProRes, MJPEG and MPEG-4 video; VP9 Profile 0 and 2 in MP4; AV1 on an M3 or later Mac. |
| WebM and Matroska | `.webm` and `.mkv` with VP9, AV1, H.264 or HEVC video and Opus, Vorbis or AAC sound (see below). |
| Sound | M4A (AAC, ALAC), MP3, WAV and AIFF everywhere. Other formats macOS plays, such as CAF and FLAC, import when dropped on the Media tab. |
| Pictures | PNG, JPEG and HEIC everywhere. TIFF, GIF, BMP, HEIF and WebP also import when dropped on the Media tab. |
| LUTs | `.cube` 3D LUTs, applied as a clip's look or as a file's Camera Log. See [Color grading](color-grading.md). |

Caption files (`.srt`) are not media: bring them in with **File ▸ Import Captions…**. See [Captions](captions.md).

### Add Media

**File ▸ Add Media…** (⇧⌘I), or the Media tab's **Add Media…** button, opens a panel for one or more files. Every file is checked first. The readable ones are added to the Media tab together as one undo step ("Add Media", or "Add 3 Media Files"). A file that cannot be read shows an alert naming it, and the rest are still added. Adding a file that is already in the list changes nothing.

Adding puts files in the Media tab, **not** on the timeline. Place them from there (see [Putting media on the timeline](#putting-media-on-the-timeline)).

You can also drag files from the Finder onto the **Media tab**. That adds them to this project. A Finder drop anywhere else on the window (the canvas, the timeline) *opens* the file as a project of its own, as a drop on the Dock icon does.

*Agents:* `import_media` (takes a `path`; answers the new media id and what the check found: kind, duration, display size, frame rate, video/audio/alpha). `add_media` is the raw op behind it, taking a descriptor you supply.

### WebM and Matroska files

macOS cannot play WebM or MKV directly, so Frame Job copies the video and sound streams into a movie, without re-encoding, the first time you add or open one. The copy goes into `~/Library/Application Support/Frame Job/Rewrapped/`; your original is left where it is.

- There is no question to answer. A copy that takes more than a second shows a small **Copying Movie** window with its progress, and **Cancel** stops it and adds nothing.
- Before copying, Frame Job checks the disk has room. If it does not: "Not enough free space to open *file*: its video and sound need about *size* on "*volume*", which has *size* free. Nothing was copied."
- The copy keeps the colour the file states: HLG, HDR10 (PQ), or a BT.709, BT.601 or BT.2020 SDR picture, read from the file's colour information or, for VP9, from the video itself. A file that states none is shown as macOS reads it.
- Importing the same file again reuses the copy.
- The media keeps the original's name, and its tooltip on the Media tab says where the copy lives.
- If the copy is later deleted, or moved to the Trash, the project makes it again from the original the next time it opens. If that copy is cancelled or fails, the file shows as missing (a slate, the **missing** badge, Relink…) until the next open tries again.
- Frame Job never deletes anything from the Rewrapped folder, which every project shares, so copies pile up there. You can clear it: WebM and MKV copies are made again on the next open (ffmpeg conversions are not; see below).
- **Consolidate Media** copies the copy, not the WebM, into the package's `media/` folder, and the row's tooltip then says it was copied into this project's package.

A stream the built-in copy cannot carry (FLAC, MP3, AC-3, MPEG-2 and similar) is refused with a sentence naming it. If you have ffmpeg installed, Frame Job then offers to help (next section).

### Files macOS cannot open, and ffmpeg

When macOS refuses a file and `ffmpeg` and `ffprobe` are both installed on this Mac, Frame Job asks before doing anything. It looks in your `PATH` first, then in `/opt/homebrew/bin`, `/usr/local/bin`, `/opt/local/bin`, `/usr/bin` and `/bin`; to use one particular build, run `defaults write com.kgalligan.FrameJob RCFFmpegPath /path/to/ffmpeg` (its `ffprobe` is taken from the same folder when one is there). The alert, "Frame Job cannot open *file*.", says what it would cost: a quick **Repackage** that copies the streams, or a **Convert** that re-encodes, with the size and the time it would take. Tick **Do this automatically from now on** to have your answer remembered: always, if you accept, or never, if you cancel. The converted file goes into the same Rewrapped folder, and the original is untouched. A conversion that fails shows "Could not convert *file* with ffmpeg: *reason*". Unlike a WebM copy, a conversion that is later deleted is not made again when the project opens: the media stays missing until you relink it. Frame Job does not ship ffmpeg; without one, this step never appears. To be asked again after ticking "Do this automatically", see [Settings](settings.md#limits).

An agent's import never shows this question. Unless you have chosen "always", the file is refused instead.

### Files that are refused

- **A codec this Mac cannot decode** is refused at import with a sentence naming it, for example "*file* is AV1 video, which needs an M3 or later Mac." or "*file* is VP9 Profile 1 video, which this Mac cannot decode; VP9 Profiles 0 and 2 import." VP8 is refused the same way. A file in a codec this Mac does decode still imports even when some of its data is damaged.
- **A `.cube` the LUT reader cannot read** is refused naming the line and the problem, for example "“Film.cube” is not a LUT Frame Job reads: line 2: LUT_3D_SIZE 200 is outside 2–65."
- "Could not read *file*." means the file is damaged or not a format Frame Job reads.
- "*file* has no video or audio the app can open." means the file holds neither.
- "Timed out reading *file*." means the check took longer than 30 seconds, usually because the file is on a stalled network volume.

## The Media tab

The inspector's **Media** tab lists every file the project has imported, in a bar, a find band, the list and a footer.

- **The top bar:** **Add Media…** (⇧⌘I) and a count: "No media", "1 item", "12 items", or "3 of 12 items" while the list is narrowed.
- **The find band:** a **Search by name** field that filters as you type, ignoring case and accents ("resume" finds "Résumé.mov"; Esc clears it), a **Sort** popup (**Import Order**, Name, Duration, Kind), and an **Unused only** checkbox that shows only files no clip uses. Every sort is ascending, and files that tie stay in import order. A file used only inside a nest counts as used. None of these is saved with the project. If nothing matches: "No media matches the search or the filter." If the search or Unused only hides the selected row, that row is deselected.
- **The footer:** **Consolidate…**, with "Copies sources into the package" beside it.

With no media yet, the tab reads "Drop files here, or use Add Media…."

### A media row

Each row shows a thumbnail (a frame for video, a waveform glyph for sound, a cube for a LUT), the file's name, and a line with what applies to that file:

| Kind | The line reads |
|---|---|
| Movie | duration · width×height · frame rate, e.g. `00:01:12:04 · 1920×1080 · 29.97 fps` |
| Picture | width×height |
| Sound | duration |
| LUT | LUT |

Badges on the right mark a file that has **audio** and a file that is **missing**. Hover a row for its tooltip: "Drag to a timeline track, or onto the canvas. Hold ⌥ to insert, ⇧⌥ to overwrite." A LUT's reads "A LUT: apply it to clips as a look." A WebM, MKV or ffmpeg copy's tooltip adds a line above with the original's path and where the copy lives.

Click a row to select it; the selected row is outlined in the accent colour. Selecting a row is not an edit and does not mark the project as changed. Two more sections appear below the list for the selected row when the project has the right kind of file:

- **Camera Log**, once the project has a video file: how the selected file's log footage is converted. See [HDR and colour](hdr-and-color.md).
- **HDR10**, once the project has a PQ file: the peak brightness used for the selected file. See [HDR and colour](hdr-and-color.md).

### Putting media on the timeline

- **Drag a row onto a timeline track.** With no modifier it lands at the pointer, snapped to a frame, if that part of the track is free; if it would overlap a clip already there, the drop is refused and the drag springs back. Hold **⌥** as you drop to *insert* (the track opens up to make room) or **⇧⌥** to *overwrite* (whatever is under it on that track is replaced).
- **Drag a row onto the canvas.** It lands on a new track at the front, at the playhead.
- **Edit ▸ Insert at Playhead** / **Edit ▸ Overwrite at Playhead** place the selected row at the playhead. They have no shortcut, and they are off until a row (not a LUT) is selected on the Media tab. The track is the selected clip's track, or the front track when no clip is selected. With a nest open, that is a track inside the nest.

A row can only be placed in its own project's window; dragged into another project's window, it is refused.

A new clip is the whole file, as long as the file runs. A picture is 5 seconds long. With **Fit new clips to canvas** on, a file larger than the canvas is scaled to fit. A LUT row cannot be dragged or placed; it is applied as a look instead. What insert and overwrite do to the clips around them is covered in [Editing](editing.md).

*Agents:* `add_clip`, `insert_clip`, `overwrite_clip` (each takes `track`, `media` and `at`).

### The row's menu

Right-click a row for:

| Item | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Insert at Playhead** | As Edit ▸ Insert at Playhead, for this row. Off for a LUT. |
| **Overwrite at Playhead** | As Edit ▸ Overwrite at Playhead, for this row. Off for a LUT. |
| **Reveal in Timeline** | Selects every clip on the timeline that shows this file and scrolls to the earliest one; the inspector switches to the Clip tab. Off when nothing on the timeline uses the file, including when its only clips are inside a nest. For a LUT, it selects the clips whose look it is. |
| **Reveal in Finder** | Shows the file in the Finder. For a WebM or MKV copy, shows the original, or the copy when the original is gone. |
| **Relink…** | Points this media at another file (see [Missing media and Relink](#missing-media-and-relink)). |
| **Remove** | Takes the file out of the project (see below). |

### Removing media

**Remove** on an unused file removes it at once, as one undo step. If clips use it, Frame Job asks first:

- For footage: "Remove "*name*"? It is used by 3 clips, which will be removed with it." **Remove and Delete Clips** removes the file and those clips, including any inside nests, as one undo step.
- For a LUT: the alert counts the clips whose look it is ("which keep their place and lose the look") and the files whose Camera Log it is ("which lose it"). **Remove and Clear Looks** removes the LUT and clears those looks and conversions; the clips stay.

Removing media never deletes the file from disk.

*Agents:* `remove_media` (refused while clips use it unless `with_clips: true`).

## Missing media and Relink

A project always opens, even when files it uses have moved or been deleted. Clips whose file is gone keep their place on the timeline and show a slate in their place, and their media rows wear the **missing** badge.

When a project opens with files missing, Frame Job offers the **Missing media** sheet once: "The project opened without these files: their clips keep their place on the timeline and show a slate until the files are found." Each missing file is listed with its old path and a **Locate…** button.

- Choosing a file for one entry also looks in that file's folder for the other missing files by name, and fills in each one it finds. A shoot moved as one folder is usually found with one Locate….
- A located row's button turns into **Change…**.
- The footnote counts the missing files ("3 files").
- **Relink** stays off until at least one file is located, then applies every choice as one undo step ("Relink Media"). You do not have to locate them all: the ones you skip stay missing, and you can relink them later from the Media tab. **Cancel** changes nothing.
- The sheet is offered once, when the window opens, and not over another sheet that is already showing.

Relinking checks the new file as an import does. The media takes the new file's duration, size, frame rate and audio/video flags. A clip that runs past the end of a shorter new file is shortened to end with it. A file of another kind (a sound file for a video entry, say) is refused, and the reason is shown after the other relinks are applied. A WebM or MKV chosen as the new file is copied as on import.

To relink one file at any time, use **Relink…** on its Media-tab row: "Choose the file for "*name*"."

A consolidated package that has been moved or renamed finds its own copies again when it opens: any missing media whose file sits in the package's `media/` folder under the same name is pointed back at it, with no sheet.

*Agents:* `relink_media` (takes `media` and `path`; the app checks the new file itself). `get_project`'s `missing_media` lists what needs it.

## Consolidate Media

**File ▸ Consolidate Media…**, or **Consolidate…** at the foot of the Media tab, copies every file in the project's media list (used on the timeline or not) into the package's `media/` folder and points the project at the copies. Afterwards the package is the whole edit: you can hand it to someone, move it, or archive it and delete the originals.

- The project must have been saved first. On an untitled project the command asks "Save this project first?" and offers **Save…**; after the save it carries on.
- A **Consolidating Media** sheet shows progress ("Copying 4 files (2.1 GB) into the package…") and the file being copied. **Cancel** stops the copying; what was copied stays copied and the rest keep pointing at the originals, so the project always opens.
- When it finishes the sheet says what happened ("Copied 4 files (2.1 GB) into the package.", plus any files that could not be copied and any missing files it left alone) and offers **Show in Finder** and **Close**. The relinks are one undo step, "Consolidate Media".
- Two files with the same name are kept apart (`intro.mov`, `intro-2.mov`). Two entries that point at the same file share one copy. Files already inside the package are not copied again.
- Missing files cannot be copied: relink them first. If there is nothing to do, it says "Nothing to consolidate." and why.
- LUTs are consolidated like footage.

The command is off when the project has no media.

*Agents:* `consolidate_media` (needs a saved project; can take a while and copies as many bytes as the footage weighs).

## Limits

- Consolidate Media needs a saved project.
- Canvas width and height are even numbers from 16 to 16384 px.
- A project holds at most 4,096 clips and 64 tracks (counting those inside nests), 1,024 markers and 1,024 media files, with nests up to 8 deep.
- The Add Media… and Open panels list movies, M4A, MP3, WAV, AIFF, PNG, JPEG, HEIC and (Add Media… only) `.cube`. Other sound and picture formats import only by a drop on the Media tab, or through `import_media`.
- `.cube` files are imported, not opened: File ▸ Open… does not take one, and a `.cube` dropped on the window or the Dock is not imported. Use Add Media… or a drop on the Media tab.
- A project file that is damaged or out of range fails to open with a message naming the problem; the package is not rewritten. A package saved by a newer Frame Job reports "project format version *N* is newer than this build understands (version *M*); update Frame Job to open it". A package with no readable `project.json` reports "*name* does not contain a readable project.json."

content.content:
- **No filmstrip**: text, shape, graphic, nest and adjustment clips have no
  thumbnails. An adjustment clip is a plain rose block with only its name
  strip and action lane, and its track is sized as a picture track.

Filmstrips and waveforms come from a cache made for each media file after
import, so they fill in a moment after a file is added.

### The action lane

A clip that has actions (keyframed segments) gets an **action lane** right
under its name strip. Each action is a band. At Medium and Large each band
shows its number in time order (and a zoom glyph for a zoom action); at Large
it also lists the properties it changes; at Small the bands are plain bars.
The selected action is solid, its span is washed down the clip, and it is
shaded on the ruler.

Hover a band to highlight it and show its 5 pt grips at both ends (a band
15 pt wide or less has none). The pointer is an open hand over the body and
a resize arrow over a grip.

Click a band to select the clip and that action; the playhead also moves to
the action's end, so the preview shows its end state. Drag a band's body to
move the action, or drag a grip to resize it. After a move or resize the
action stays selected and the playhead goes to its new end. When exactly one
clip is selected, playing or scrubbing into one of its actions' spans
selects that action. Esc leaves it, and ⌫ removes it.
Everything else about actions is on
[Motion and transitions](motion-and-transitions.md).

## The ruler and the playhead

The ruler's ticks adjust to the zoom, from single frames up to minutes.
Labels drop the hours when the timeline is under an hour long. The playhead
is the coral line with a triangle head on the ruler.

- **Click the ruler** to move the playhead there, and **drag** along it to
  scrub. Playback stops while you scrub, and you hear the sound under the
  playhead instead (see [Hearing a scrub](audio.md#hearing-a-scrub)). The
  scrub snaps like any other drag
  (see [Snapping](#snapping)).
- The timeline scrolls itself to keep the playhead in view: when the playhead
  leaves the visible part, during playback or after a jump, the view moves
  so the playhead sits about a third of the way in.
- A click in a lane doesn't move the playhead. It starts a marquee selection
  (see [Selecting clips](#selecting-clips)).

## Playback

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| Space | Play / pause |
| J | Play backwards; press again for 2×, then 4× |
| K | Pause |
| L | Play forwards; press again for 2×, then 4× |
| ← / → | Back / forward one frame (pauses) |
| ⇧← / ⇧→ | Back / forward ten frames |
| ↑ / ↓ | Previous / next edit point |
| Home / End | Go to the start / end |

**Edit points** are the start and end of the timeline and the start and end
of every clip. ↑ with nothing earlier goes to the start.

J pressed while playing forwards, or L while playing backwards, switches
direction at 1×.

Space plays and pauses wherever the focus is, except while you type in a
text field or when a focused button uses the key itself. Typing ends with
Return, Tab or a click outside the field (on the timeline, say), and Space
plays straight after it. On the preview
canvas a quick Space press still plays or pauses (when you let go), while
holding Space and dragging pans the canvas instead. Holding Space down
doesn't toggle playback over and over. Letter keys never
fire while you are typing in a field, and no editor key works while a sheet
is open.

Playback stops at the end of the timeline. An empty timeline has nothing to
play: Play beeps.

### Loop

Turn on **Loop** in the toolbar to loop playback. With an in/out range set it
loops the range; otherwise it loops the whole timeline. Pressing play at or
past the end of the loop starts again from the loop's start. Loop is set per
window and isn't saved.

### What you'll notice after an edit

- A change that only alters how something looks (a property, a colour, text)
  redraws the frame in place without interrupting playback.
- A change to the timeline's structure (a move, a trim, a new clip) rebuilds
  the player in the background. It keeps your place and keeps playing at the
  same rate. While you drag, the rebuild waits until you pause briefly.
- If a rebuild fails, an error is shown and the previous version keeps
  playing.

*Agents:* `set_playhead {t}` moves the playhead and seeks the preview.
`get_project` reports the playhead, selection and in/out range along with the
project. `render_frame` writes the frame at a time as a PNG.

## Zooming the timeline

| Way | How |
|---|---|
| Pinch | On a trackpad, about the pointer |
| ⌥-scroll or ⌘-scroll | Zoom about the pointer |
| Zoom slider | The slider in the timeline bar |
| − / + buttons | Either side of the slider, in steps about the middle of the view |
| Fit Timeline | ⇧Z, the ⇔ button, or **View ▸ Fit Timeline**. Fits the whole timeline in the view and scrolls to the start. |

A window opens at a fixed zoom of about 42 pt per second, not fitted to the
project, so press ⇧Z to see all of a long project. The zoom runs from about a
third of a point per second (hours on screen) to 4,000 pt per second (single
frames wide).

A plain scroll moves the view. **View ▸ Zoom In** (⌘+ or ⌘=), **Zoom Out**
(⌘-) and **Zoom to Fit** (⌘0) zoom the *preview*, not the timeline. They step
through the same stops as the toolbar's zoom popup (see
[Canvas and layers](canvas-and-layers.md)).

## Selecting clips

| To | Do this |
|---|---|
| Select a clip | Click it |
| Add or remove a clip | ⇧-click it |
| Select with a marquee | Drag from any empty space: a gap in a lane, the strip under the ruler, or the space below the last lane. A plain drag replaces the selection; ⇧-drag adds to it. Clips on locked tracks are skipped. |
| Clear the selection | Click empty space |
| Select everything | **Edit ▸ Select All** (⌘A): every clip, on locked tracks too |
| Select everything from the playhead on | **Edit ▸ Select After Playhead** (⌥⌘A): every clip whose start is at or after the playhead, on every track including locked ones. A clip under the playhead isn't included. |
| Select a track's clips | ⌥-click its header, or **Edit ▸ Select All on Track** |

The **selection block** at the left of the timeline bar names what is
selected: one clip's name over its track and kind (`Track 2 · video`), or a
count such as `3 clips` over the track (or `2 tracks`) and the kind (or
`mixed`). With nothing selected it reads "No selection". Selecting clips on
the timeline switches the inspector to its Clip tab.

**Edit ▸ Select All on Track** selects every clip on the current track: the
first selected clip's track, or the front track when nothing is selected. It
beeps when that track is empty. ⌥-clicking a header uses the track you
clicked.

Selection is view state: it is never an undo step and isn't saved.

*Agents:* `set_selection {clips}` (an empty list selects nothing).

## Snapping

Snapping is on by default. While on, a drag (move, trim, roll, marker or
scrub) jumps to a nearby **clip edge**, **marker**, **the playhead**,
**an in/out point**, or **the start or end of the timeline** when it comes within about 8 pt, and a thin guide line
shows what it caught. A drag that doesn't snap still lands on a whole frame.

| To | Do this |
|---|---|
| Turn snapping on or off | N, the **Snap** checkbox in the timeline bar, or **View ▸ Snapping** (checked when on) |
| Skip snapping for one drag | Hold ⌘ while you drag |

The setting is remembered between launches.

## Markers

Markers are flags on the ruler at project time. A **chapter marker** is
drawn as a filled flag and also becomes a chapter in exported movies (see
[Export](export.md)); an ordinary marker is an outline.

| To | Do this |
|---|---|
| Add a marker at the playhead | M, the bookmark button in the timeline bar, or **Mark ▸ Add Marker** |
| Move one | Drag its flag along the ruler (it snaps) |
| Rename one | Double-click its flag, or type in its row in the Document tab |
| Make it a chapter | Tick **Chapter** in its Document-tab row |
| Jump to one | **Mark ▸ Next Marker** / **Previous Marker**, or **Go** in its Document-tab row |
| Remove one | **Delete** in its Document-tab row |

The Document tab's **Markers** section lists every marker in time order with
its time, its name, **Chapter**, **Go** and **Delete**. With none it says
"No markers. Press M to add one."

A new marker is called `Marker N` and is red. Two markers can't share a frame,
so M on a frame that already has a marker beeps, and a drag onto another
marker's frame doesn't move it. **Next Marker** and **Previous Marker** pause
playback and jump; they beep when there is no marker further in that
direction, and are dimmed when the project has no markers.

Markers belong to the whole timeline. While a nest is open the ruler shows no
markers and drags don't snap to them, the three Mark ▸ marker commands are
off (a bare M beeps), and **Go** is disabled (the playhead inside a nest
counts from the nest's own start). The Document tab's Markers list still
shows every marker, and its name field, **Chapter** and **Delete** still
work.

A marker's colour is set only through an agent. The names are the six label
colours (below); any other name draws in the neutral text colour.

*Agents:* `add_marker {at?, name?, chapter?, color?}` (at the playhead when
`at` is left out), `set_marker {marker, time?, name?, chapter?, color?}`,
`remove_marker {marker}`.

## The in/out range

The in/out range is a span of the timeline shaded across the ruler and the
lanes. It sets what Loop plays, what ⌫ lifts and ⌘⌫ ripple-deletes when no
clip is selected (see [Editing](editing.md)), the span a speed ramp preset
covers when it lies inside the clip (see [Speed](speed.md)), what a new
adjustment clip covers (see [Colour grading](color-grading.md)), and what an
export writes when you choose the range.

| Key | Menu | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| I | **Mark ▸ Set In** | Sets the in point at the playhead. With no range yet, the out point goes to the end of the timeline. |
| O | **Mark ▸ Set Out** | Sets the out point at the playhead. With no range yet, the in point goes to the start. |
| ⌥X | **Mark ▸ Clear Range** | Clears the range (available only while one is set) |

Setting an in point after the out point moves the out point to match, and
the other way round. The range is view state (not an undo step, not saved),
and it's cleared whenever you enter or leave a nest.

*Agents:* `set_range {start?, end?}` (no bounds clears it).

## Clip names and labels

**Rename a clip in place**: double-click it on the timeline, or select it
and choose **Clip ▸ Rename…** (⇧⌘R). A field opens over its name strip; the
timeline scrolls it into view first if needed. Return, Tab or a click
elsewhere saves the name as its own undo step; Esc closes the field and keeps
the old name. Saving an empty field or an unchanged name does nothing. To
clear a name back to what the clip shows, use the name field at the top of
the Clip tab. Double-clicking a nest clip opens the nest instead, so rename a
nest with ⇧⌘R or the Clip tab.

The same field renames tracks (double-click the header) and markers
(double-click the flag).

**Label a clip** with **Clip ▸ Label ▸**: Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue,
Purple, or None to remove it. It applies to every selected clip. The menu
checks the label when all the selected clips share it. Labels are for your
own sorting; they don't change how the clip plays or exports.

*Agents:* `set_clip {clips, patch}` with `name` and `label` in the patch (a
null or blank name clears it).

## Finding a file's clips

In the Media tab, right-click a file and choose **Reveal in Timeline**. It
selects every timeline clip that uses the file and scrolls the first one into
view. The item is disabled when the file is used only inside a nest (open the
nest to reach those clips). See [Projects and media](projects-and-media.md).

## Inside a nest

While a nest is open the timeline shows the nest's own tracks and clips from
its own zero, and the corner above the track headers shows the path back, for
example `Timeline › Intro` (hover for the full path). Click it, or press ⌘↑
(**Clip ▸ Close Nest**), to come back out one level. Entering a nest is
covered in [Editing](editing.md).

## The level meter

The two-channel meter in the timeline bar shows the mix while the project
plays and drops to silence when it stops. In a narrow window it gets smaller
and can disappear. It's described on [Audio](audio.md).

## The preview

### Preview Quality

**View ▸ Preview Quality ▸** Full, Half or Quarter draws the preview at a
fraction of the canvas size and scales it back up to fit. It makes heavy
projects play more smoothly. It never changes an export, a saved frame or a
rendered frame. The menu checks the current choice, Full is the default, and
the choice is remembered. The Preview Window (below) shows the same player,
so it draws at the same quality.

### A second preview window

**View ▸ Preview Window** (⇧⌘P) opens the picture in its own window, titled
"<project> — Preview", with no handles or guides drawn over it. Use it to
put the picture on a second display; it can go full screen. It shows the same
player as the main preview, so the two never drift apart. The menu item has a
checkmark while the window is open, and the same key hides it again. The
window remembers where you put it and stays visible when you switch to
another app. While it has the focus, the playback keys and the editor's other
bare keys still work, and so does Undo. It closes with its project window.

### Other View items for the preview

- **View ▸ Safe Areas**: the same title-safe / action-safe guides as the
  toolbar's **Safe** checkbox (checked when on).
- **View ▸ Show Ungraded** (⌃⌘U), **Show Selection** and **Scopes** (⌃⌘W):
  see [Colour grading](color-grading.md).
- **View ▸ Show SDR Version**: see [HDR and colour management](hdr-and-color.md).
- **View ▸ Assistant** (⌃⌘A): see [Assistant](assistant.md).

## What is remembered

| Setting | Remembered between launches |
|---|---|
| Timeline height, inspector width, inspector hidden | Yes |
| Snapping, track size, Safe Areas, Preview Quality | Yes, for every project |
| Preview Window position | Yes |
| Timeline zoom, Loop, playhead, selection, in/out range | No |

## Limits

- Markers live on the main timeline only. Inside a nest the ruler shows
  none, drags don't snap to them, and you can't add one, step to one or jump
  to one; the Document tab can still rename, chapter and delete them.
- Clips on a locked track can be clicked and selected, but not dragged or
  trimmed, and a marquee skips them.
- A marker's colour can only be changed by an agent.
- The timeline zoom has no menu item or keyboard shortcut except ⇧Z (fit).

See [Menus and shortcuts](menus-and-shortcuts.md) for every key in one place.

# The timeline and playback

The editor window shows your project in four areas: the toolbar, the
preview, the inspector and the timeline. This page covers how to move around
the timeline and play the project back: tracks and their switches, the ruler
and playhead, zoom and row heights, selection, snapping, markers, the in/out
range, clip names and labels, and the View menu items for the timeline and
the preview. Editing with gestures (moving, trimming, slipping and so on) is
on [Editing](editing.md).

## The editor window

| Area | Where | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| Title bar | top | The project name, with canvas size, frame rate and "edited" (while unsaved) as the subtitle, e.g. `1920 × 1080 · 30 fps · edited` |
| Toolbar | under the title bar | Transport, timecode, preview zoom, safe-area guides, **Export…** |
| Preview | middle left | The frame under the playhead, at canvas size, letterboxed |
| Inspector | middle right | The Clip, Media, Document and Assistant tabs |
| Timeline bar | above the timeline | The selection block, clip buttons, Snap, the level meter, zoom, track size (see [below](#the-timeline-bar)) |
| Timeline | bottom | The ruler, track headers and lanes |

Drag the dividers to resize the panes. The inspector can be 280–440 pt wide
(304 pt to start) and the timeline 140 pt up to 60 % of the window (300 pt to
start). The sizes you drag to are remembered. Dragging the inspector divider
to the edge stops at its minimum width; the only way to hide the inspector is
**View ▸ Hide Inspector** (⌥⌘I), which becomes **Show Inspector** while it is
hidden and is also remembered. The window is at least 900 × 620 pt.

### The toolbar

From left to right:

- **Transport**: Go to Start (Home), Previous Edit Point (↑), Play / Pause
  (Space), Next Edit Point (↓), Go to End (End), and **Loop**. Loop is dimmed
  while off.
- **Timecode**: the playhead's time, then `/` and the duration of what the
  timeline shows. Click the time to type one: it takes `HH:MM:SS:FF`,
  `HH:MM:SS.mmm`, `HH:MM:SS`, `MM:SS`, seconds with a decimal (`83.5`) or a
  bare number of seconds. Press Return to jump there, snapped to a frame.
  Text that is not a time beeps and the field goes back to the playhead's
  time.
- **Preview zoom**: a popup with Fit, 50%, 100% and 200%.
- **Safe**: shows the title-safe and action-safe guides (90 % and 80 %
  rectangles) on the preview. Remembered between launches.
- **Export…** (⌘E): see [Export](export.md).

Timecode shows frames by default. The Document tab's **Timecode** popup
(Frames or Milliseconds) changes every readout, the ruler included.

### The timeline bar

From left to right:

- **The selection block**, naming what is selected (see
  [Selecting clips](#selecting-clips)).
- **Eight clip buttons**: Split (⌘T), Trim Start to Playhead (W), Trim End
  to Playhead (E), Ripple Delete (⌘⌫), Add Marker (M), Duplicate (⌘D), Add
  Text (T) and Add Shape. Each button's tooltip names its key. **Add Shape**
  opens a menu of shapes and has no menu-bar item, so this button is the way
  to add one. What the edits do is on [Editing](editing.md); text and shapes
  are on [Canvas and layers](canvas-and-layers.md).
- **Snap**, the snapping checkbox (see [Snapping](#snapping)).
- **The level meter** (see [The level meter](#the-level-meter)).
- **The zoom cluster**: −, the zoom slider, + and Fit (⇔) (see
  [Zooming the timeline](#zooming-the-timeline)).
- **S / M / L**, the track size (see [Row heights](#row-heights)).

## Tracks

There is one kind of track, and it holds any clip: video, audio, a still,
text, a shape, a graphic, a nest or an adjustment clip. Tracks stack: **the
top lane is the front-most**, and the bottom lane is the back.

### Track headers

Each track has a header on the left with its name and five switches:

| Switch | Symbol (off / on) | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Hide Video | eye / struck-through eye | Takes the track's picture out of the preview and export. Its clips draw dimmed. |
| Mute Audio | speaker / crossed-out speaker | Silences the track's sound. |
| Lock Track | open padlock / closed padlock | Protects the track from edits: its clips can't be dragged or trimmed, a marquee skips them, and ripple, insert and range edits leave them alone. The lane is hatched. |
| Solo | headphones (both) | Silences every other track that is not soloed too. Pictures stay. Mute still wins on a track that is both muted and soloed. |
| Mix | sliders (both) | Opens the track's mix panel: volume, pan, compressor and limiter ([Audio](audio.md#track-volume-and-pan)). Lit while the volume or pan is not at its default, or a compressor or limiter is on. |

A lit switch is also highlighted in the accent colour, so you can read a
track's state from the symbol or the highlight. Under a solo, the waveforms
on the silenced tracks draw faded but their speakers stay unlit, because the
speaker shows the track's own setting.

A track with no name shows `Track N`, counting up from the back track.

### Managing tracks

| To | Do this |
|---|---|
| Add a track at the front | **Track ▸ New Track** (⇧⌘N) |
| Rename a track | Double-click its name in the header |
| Reorder | Drag a header up or down. A coral line shows where it will land. |
| Select every clip on a track | ⌥-click its header, or **Edit ▸ Select All on Track** (the current track, below) |
| Remove a track | **Track ▸ Remove Track**, or the header's context menu |
| Drop every empty track | **Track ▸ Remove Empty Tracks** |

Dragging a clip above the top lane or below the bottom lane makes a new track
for it (see [Editing](editing.md)).

**Remove Track** removes an empty track at once. If the track still holds
clips it asks first ("The track still holds 3 clips, which will be removed
with it.") with **Remove** and **Cancel**. The last track can't be removed.
**Remove Empty Tracks** always keeps at least one track.

The **Track** menu works on the *current track*: the first selected clip's
track, or the front-most track when nothing is selected. Besides the commands
above it has **Hide Video**, **Mute Audio**, **Lock Track** and **Solo**,
which flip that track's switches, and **Mix…**, which opens the
track's mix panel. Only Solo shows a checkmark there. The
**Matte ▸** submenu is described in
[Canvas and layers](canvas-and-layers.md).

### The track context menu

Right-click (or ⌃-click) a header, or an empty part of a lane, to get that
track's menu: **Hide Video**, **Mute Audio**, **Lock Track** and **Solo**,
each checked when on, then **Mix…**, then **Matte ▸**, then
**Remove Track** (disabled on the last track). Right-clicking a clip opens no menu.

Every switch flip, rename and reorder is one undo step. The names **Edit ▸
Undo** shows for this page's edits are:

| Edit | Undo name |
|---|---|
| Track switches | Hide Track, Mute Track, Lock Track, Solo Track |
| A track's matte | Track Matte |
| A track's volume and pan | Track Volume, Track Pan, Reset Track Mix |
| Track names and order | Rename Track, Reorder Track |
| Adding and removing tracks | New Track, Remove Track, Remove Empty Tracks |
| Markers | Add Marker, Move Marker, Rename Marker, Chapter Marker, Remove Marker |
| Clip names and labels | Rename Clip, Label Clip |

*Agents:* `add_track` (an `index`, 0 being the back; the front when left
out), `remove_track` (`with_clips` to take its clips too), `move_track`,
`set_track` (`name`, `hidden`, `muted`, `locked`, `solo`, `matte`, `volume`,
`pan`), `remove_empty_tracks`.

### Row heights

Pick the track size with the **S / M / L** control at the right end of the
timeline bar, or **View ▸ Timeline Track Height ▸** Small, Medium or Large.
Medium is the default and your choice is remembered.

Each track's height also depends on what it holds:

| Track holds | Small | Medium | Large |
|---|---|---|---|
| Only text and shapes | 30 pt | 44 pt | 58 pt |
| Only clips with sound and no picture | 40 pt | 60 pt | 82 pt |
| Anything else (an empty track included) | 54 pt | 84 pt | 116 pt |

At Small a clip shows little more than its name strip.

## Reading a clip

Each clip is drawn as one rounded block with a thin border, so you can see
where one ends and the next begins.

- **Colour by kind**: video slate, audio green, image or still violet, text
  amber, shape teal (graphics use the same colour), nest grey, adjustment
  rose.
- **Name strip** along the top: a symbol for the kind, then the clip's name.
  A clip with no name of its own shows what it holds: its file, its text, its
  shape or its nest.
- **Label dot**: a labelled clip gets a small dot in its label colour at the
  right end of the name strip. The block's colour still shows its kind.
- **Filmstrip**: thumbnails along the picture part of a video or image clip,
  under a wash of the clip's colour. Each thumbnail is the source frame at
  that point, following speed, reverse and speed ramps.
- **Waveform**: the sound of a clip that has audio, drawn below the
  filmstrip on a clip that has both. Muted, or silenced by another track's
  solo, it draws faded.
- **Fade handles**: small white squares at the top corners of the audio part.
  Drag one inward to fade (see [Audio](audio.md)).
- **Volume line**: a thin white line over the waveform showing the level you
  hear from the clip, with small squares where a volume action ends. Drag it
  to change the level, or ⌥-click it to add a point (see
  [Audio](audio.md#the-volume-line)). A silenced clip's line lies along the
  bottom.
- **Motion marks**: small wedges at the ends of the name strip for an active
  In or Out motion, and a wave glyph for a During motion (see
  [Motion and transitions](motion-and-transitions.md)).
- **Transitions**: the overlap between two clips is hatched, with the
  transition's kind written in it when the word fits.
- **Selected**: a 2 pt coral ring, with trim grips at both ends when the clip
  is wide enough to trim and its track is unlocked.
- **Linked**: a picture and the sound Detach Audio split from it each show a
  link symbol after the kind symbol. When one is selected, the other gets a
  dashed accent ring, because edits to one move both (see
  [Audio](audio.md#what-stays-in-sync)).
- **Dimmed**: a clip on a hidden track, or one with both its picture and its
  sound switched off.
- **No filmstrip**: text, shape, graphic, nest and adjustment clips have no

content.content:
# Remove Silences and Remove Filler Words

Frame Job has two commands for cleaning up a spoken recording such as a screencast, a tutorial or a talking-head take. **Remove Silences** finds the dead air and cuts it. **Remove Filler Words** finds the ums and uhs and cuts them on the words' own timings. Both show what they would cut before they cut anything, and both make the whole cut as one undo step. An agent can read the same answers, and it can read a clip's transcript to cut false starts.

Both commands are in the **Clip** menu, after **Close Gap**. Neither has a keyboard shortcut.

## How a clean-up cut works

The two commands cut the same way:

- **Preview first.** While the sheet is open, each span it would remove is shaded on the timeline ruler and lanes, and the sheet reads, for example, "23 cuts · removes 00:00:04:12". With nothing to cut it reads "No cuts" and **Remove** is disabled. The shading goes away when the sheet closes.
- **One edit.** **Remove** cuts every span and closes the timeline over each one, all as a single undo step: **Undo Remove Silences** or **Undo Remove Filler Words**. One ⌘Z restores everything.
- **Across the timeline.** A cut is a ripple delete across every **unlocked** track, not just the clips that were analysed, so the picture above a voice-over is cut with it. Locked tracks are neither cut nor moved.
- **Markers stay where they are.** The sheet's footnote says "markers keep their place."
- **Frame-accurate edges.** Each cut's start rounds up to the next frame and its end rounds down. That way a cut can leave up to a frame of room tone behind, but it never clips the start of the next word.
- **Nests and transitions are protected.** A cut never reaches into a nest clip, because a nest always plays from its first frame and cutting into one would strand the rest of it. A cut also never reaches into a transition's overlap or the area around it. To clean up the audio inside a nest, open it first (**Clip ▸ Open Nest**, ⌘↓) and run the command there, or un-nest it (**Clip ▸ Un-nest**, ⇧⌘G). With a nest open, both commands work on the nest's own timeline.
- **The rest of the editor waits.** Playback pauses when a sheet opens, and other editing commands are unavailable until you close it.

## Remove Silences

**Clip ▸ Remove Silences…** opens the Remove Silences sheet. The command is available whenever the timeline has a clip whose sound is switched on.

### What "silent" means

Silence is measured in the **mix**, as you hear it, not in the raw file:

- A clip you have turned down, faded out, ducked, muted, or silenced by soloing another track is quiet. It never keeps a cut from happening.
- A stretch where *every* clip in scope is quiet counts as silent. A music bed under a voice-over therefore keeps the pauses in the speech from being cut, unless you limit the scope to the voice clip (see **In:** below).
- A gap with nothing audible in it is left alone. Remove Silences takes dead air out of a recording; it does not close the gaps you placed between clips. **Clip ▸ Close Gap** does that.
- A muted clip is left out of the analysis entirely. A muted music bed is never read as one long silence covering the whole song.

### Judge by Voice or Level

**Judge by:** picks how a moment is tested.

| Mode | What counts as quiet | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Voice | Nobody is talking. An on-device voice-activity model listens to each media file once and keeps its answer with the project. A quiet microphone isn't mistaken for silence, and a hum isn't mistaken for speech. | Yes |
| Level | The sound in the mix is quieter than the threshold. | Used when the voice model can't be used |

In Voice mode, a clip with no voice in it at all, such as music or a tone, is judged by level instead. The sheet names each such clip, for example "Intro music at 00:00:12:00 holds no voice and is judged by level." That is why, in Voice mode, the threshold row is labelled **Level if no voice:**.

If the voice model can't be used on this Mac, the sheet opens in Level mode with Voice greyed out and says "The voice model could not be used, so quiet is judged by level." This lasts until you relaunch Frame Job.

Voice analysis runs on your Mac. Nothing is uploaded.

### The controls

| Control | What it does | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Judge by:** | Voice or Level, as above. | Voice | n/a |
| **Quieter than:** (Level mode) / **Level if no voice:** (Voice mode) | A slider in whole dBFS, with the value shown beside it. In Level mode, sound at or below it is quiet. In Voice mode, it judges clips that hold no voice, and a clip the mix turns down below it is quiet whatever it contains. | −40 dBFS | −80 to −10 dBFS |
| **Longer than:** | The shortest quiet stretch worth cutting, in seconds. Shorter pauses, such as the gap between two words, are kept. | 0.5 s | 0.05 to 10 s |
| **Keep at ends:** | How much of each quiet stretch to keep at each end, in seconds, so speech doesn't start or end abruptly. A stretch shorter than twice this value is not cut. | 0.1 s | 0 to 2 s |
| **In:** | **Selected clips** analyses only the selected clips. **All audible clips** analyses everything you can hear. | Selected clips when the selection includes something audible, otherwise All audible clips | n/a |

**Selected clips** is greyed out when nothing selected makes a sound. A number outside a field's range is refused: the field keeps the text and won't accept it, and **Remove** beeps, until you type a number inside the range (0.05–10 s for **Longer than:**, 0–2 s for **Keep at ends:**). The count and the shading update as you change any control.

The voice model's confidence level is not in the sheet. Agents can set it (see below).

### Notes the sheet can show

A second line explains results that a bare count would hide:

- **Nothing to analyse.** "Nothing the selected clips play is audible in the mix…" or "Nothing in this timeline is audible…"
- **Analysis still running.** "The waveform is still being analysed for …" or "Speech is still being analysed for …", naming the files. Right after you import or open a project, the app may still be analysing its files. In Level mode, nothing inside a file is proposed until its waveform is ready. In Voice mode, nothing inside a file is proposed until its voice analysis is ready, and a clip with no voice in it also waits for the waveform. Either way, a part the mix has turned down far enough to be quiet can still be proposed. The sheet updates on its own as each file finishes, so you can wait with it open. Relinking a file starts its analysis again; an open sheet drops the old answers at once and updates when the new ones land.
- **Judged by level.** In Voice mode, the clips that hold no voice.
- **Nests.** "Quiet inside a nest is left alone… Open the nest (⌘↓) and remove its silences there to take the dead air out." This appears when a nest held enough quiet to have been cut.

*Agents:* `detect_silence` answers the same ranges the sheet would cut and changes nothing. It takes `clips` (the Selected clips scope; leave it out to use the sheet's opening rule), `mode` (`voice` or `level`), `voice_confidence` (0.1–0.9, default 0.5, Voice mode only), `threshold_db` (at or below 0), and `min_length` and `padding` (in ticks, 600,000 per second). Pass its `ranges` to `ripple_delete_ranges` to make the cut. It also answers `count`, `removes` (ticks), `scope` (`selected` or `audible`), `clips`, `mode`, `judged_by_level_clips`, `voice_pending`, `proposed_by_mix_clips` when the mix alone makes a waiting clip quiet, and `protected_nests` (the nest clips a quiet run crossed, left uncut; open one with `set_scope` and call again to look for dead air inside it). Files still being analysed are listed under `pending_peaks`; call again shortly. `voice_confidence` is refused in Level mode, and `mode: "voice"` is refused when the voice model can't be used.

## Remove Filler Words

**Clip ▸ Remove Filler Words…** finds filler words in your speech and cuts them. It is available when the timeline has a clip that plays sound from a media file.

### Which words are fillers

A word counts as a filler when, lowercased and with punctuation stripped from its ends, it is one of:

um · uh · hmm · mhm · uh-huh · ah · huh · hm · m · er · erm

"Uh huh" written as two words matches as two fillers. The list is fixed, so a real "ah", "er" or the letter "M" is also treated as a filler.

### What it cuts

There is nothing to tune. Each run of consecutive fillers becomes one cut:

- The cut widens outward to a 32 ms speech grid so the whole filler goes, but it never reaches into the words on either side.
- Its edges then snap inward to the frame grid, as Remove Silences does. A tiny filler can end up too short to cut.
- A filler is **left in whole**, never trimmed, when cutting it would reach into a word spoken in another clip on any unlocked track, into a nest clip, or into a transition. The sheet counts these: "2 fillers are left in: too short to cut, or cutting would reach another clip's word, a nest or a transition."
- A clip on a locked track isn't read, because the cut can neither cut nor move it. The sheet says how many such clips there are.
- A clip that plays in reverse, whose sound is switched off, whose media file is missing, or whose media has no audio track has no words to read. When nothing in scope plays speech from a media file, the sheet says "Nothing in scope plays speech from a media file, so nothing was read."

**Which clips:** the selected clips when the selection includes speech from a media file (the sheet then says "Only the selected clips are read."), otherwise every clip. There is no scope menu.

### Filler words need a cloud transcript

Filler words come only from an **AssemblyAI** transcript made with filler words. Transcription on your Mac doesn't report them reliably. This makes filler removal a cloud feature: you need an AssemblyAI API key, set in **Frame Job ▸ Settings…** (⌘,) under **Transcription**.

Every AssemblyAI transcription Frame Job makes asks for filler words. Any file you caption with AssemblyAI (**File ▸ Generate Captions…**, AssemblyAI engine) is therefore already ready for Remove Filler Words, with no second upload. Only files never transcribed in the cloud, or transcribed before filler words were requested, are listed in the sheet.

When a file in scope has no such transcript, the sheet lists it under "Filler words are found only in an AssemblyAI transcript made with filler words — transcription on this Mac does not report them. These files have none yet:". Each listed file gets a row with:

- its name;
- the estimate: what would be uploaded and what it would cost, at the rate shown in the tooltip;
- a **Transcribe** button.

Above the rows, the sheet says where the audio goes: "The audio of these files is uploaded to AssemblyAI (United States), transcribed with Universal-3.5 Pro, and deleted from AssemblyAI once the words have been read back. Nothing is uploaded until Transcribe is pressed." It names European Union instead when that region is set in Settings.

Pressing **Transcribe** sends one file:

- It reuses that file's earlier transcription choices (language, speaker labels and vocabulary) and adds filler words. A file never transcribed before uses language detection, no speakers and no vocabulary.
- A file listed here that already has a caption transcript is uploaded again: that older transcript was made without filler words, so this is a second paid transcription.
- It only updates the project's saved transcript for that file. It places no captions and adds no undo step.
- The new transcript also serves captions: a later **File ▸ Generate Captions…** with AssemblyAI reuses it for that file instead of uploading again.
- While it runs, the row shows its progress, its button reads **Stop**, the other rows' buttons are disabled, and **Remove** is disabled. Return can't make a cut in the middle of a paid upload.
- When it finishes, the file drops off the list and its fillers join the count. If the run failed, the reason appears in the note.

**Transcribe** is disabled with no API key (the note points to **Frame Job ▸ Settings…**), for a file no clip plays, and while another file's run is going. A project you haven't saved yet can be transcribed; its transcript is kept with the project when you save. Closing the sheet stops a run in progress.

### Captions stay clean

Filler words never reach your captions. **File ▸ Generate Captions…** removes them from every transcript before making captions, so a transcript made with filler words produces the same captions as one made without them. See [Captions](captions.md).

*Agents:* `detect_fillers` answers the ranges the sheet would cut and changes nothing. It takes `clips` and lists each kept run under `fillers`, each left-in run under `dropped` with its reason, files with no filler transcript under `needs_transcript`, and locked clips under `locked`. It also answers `count`, `removes`, `scope` and `clips`, plus `skipped` when `clips` is given (each named clip it couldn't read, with the reason). Pass its `ranges` to `ripple_delete_ranges`. `transcribe_for_fillers` (`media`) is the Transcribe button: a paid upload that answers `ready` when `detect_fillers` can read that file. On a media that already has a filler transcript it uploads nothing and answers `ready: true`; otherwise it answers `uploaded`, `cached`, `audio_seconds`, `engine` and `language`. It is refused with no AssemblyAI key and for a media no clip plays. The built-in assistant can't use it.

## Reading a clip's transcript

An agent can read the words of any clip that plays speech from a media file, each with its start and end in timeline time. The times can be passed directly to a cut.

- **Where the words come from.** The file's saved AssemblyAI transcript when it has a current one. Otherwise this Mac's own speech recogniser runs over the clip, which takes a few seconds per minute of speech. Reading a transcript never uses the network and never uploads anything.
- **Fillers are flagged.** Each word says whether it is a filler. The answer also says whether the transcript was made with filler words at all. An on-device transcript never is, so a filler can be in the audio but missing from the words.
- **A part of the clip.** A `from`/`to` window in timeline time returns only the words that overlap it; a word crossing an edge comes back whole. With a window, the on-device recogniser hears only that part plus 2 seconds on each side. It is faster, but with less context a windowed answer can differ slightly from a whole-clip one. Either end may be given alone: a missing `from` is the clip's start and a missing `to` its end. The window is clamped to the clip and echoed back as `from`/`to`. An empty window, or one outside the clip, is refused.
- **Saved for next time.** What the on-device recogniser heard is saved in the project, per media file and language. A later request inside a stretch it has already heard comes back at once, even from another clip of the same file at any speed. A saved on-device transcript is used only while the media file and the macOS version are unchanged (the recogniser ships with macOS).
- **Speed and ramps.** Words are placed through the clip's speed, including a speed ramp, so their times match what plays on the timeline.
- **Stopping a read.** An on-device read can be long. The assistant's **Stop** ends it, and nothing is saved from a stopped read.
- **Language.** On-device recognition uses this Mac's language unless another tag (such as `en-US`) is given. A language whose speech model isn't installed is refused. Agents never download one; you can install it from **File ▸ Generate Captions…**.

*Agents:* `get_transcript` (`clip`, optional `language`, `from`, `to`) answers `words` (`text`, `start`, `end`, `filler`, and `speaker` when known), `fillers_reported`, `engine` and, for an on-device answer, `cached`. It edits nothing.

## Cutting false starts with the assistant

A false start is a phrase the speaker abandoned or said again. Deciding what counts is a judgement about meaning, so there is no menu command for it. Ask the assistant in the inspector's Assistant tab instead, for example "cut the false start at the beginning of this clip." The assistant:

1. reads the clip's words and their times;
2. tells you which words it will cut;
3. cuts them in one step, each cut running from the first cut word's start to the last cut word's end.

It cuts false starts only when you ask. It can also remove fillers the same way **Remove Filler Words** does, and take out silences the way **Remove Silences** does (`detect_silence`, then one `ripple_delete_ranges`). Any cut an agent makes this way, whether silences, fillers or false starts, is one undo step labelled **Undo Ripple Delete**, not the sheet's name. The assistant can't start a paid filler transcription: press **Transcribe** in the sheet yourself. See [The assistant](assistant.md).

## Limits

- **Filler removal is cloud-only.** Without an AssemblyAI key, filler words can't be found. A project transcribed before filler words were requested is transcribed again, and billed again, before its fillers can be cut.
- **The service can miss a filler.** A filler AssemblyAI doesn't return isn't cut. A filler it returns that isn't on the list stays in, both in the cut and in captions.
- **Protection needs a transcript.** A filler cut is kept away from speech in another clip only when that clip's file has a transcript. Speech on another unlocked track with no transcript isn't protected.
- **Up to a frame can remain.** Inward frame snapping can leave a frame of room tone, or of a filler, behind.
- **Wait for analysis.** After import, Remove Silences proposes nothing inside a file until its analysis is ready: the waveform in Level mode, the voice analysis in Voice mode (and the waveform too for a clip with no voice), except where the mix already makes it quiet.
- **Voice mode can miss a soft first word** in a quiet recording; raise **Keep at ends:** if a word is clipped.
- **Singing and voice-like instruments** may read as speech.
- **A clip that holds any voice is judged by voice for its whole length**, so a long music clip with a little speech in it isn't judged by level. Limit the scope (**In:** Selected clips) to keep music out.
- **A voice panned hard to one side** sounds quieter to the voice model.
- **In a reversed clip** a cut edge can be off by up to 32 ms.
- **Nests and transitions block cuts.** Quiet or fillers inside a nest, or in a transition's overlap, are never cut from outside the nest. Open the nest first.

See also: [Editing](editing.md) for ripple delete and Close Gap, [Audio](audio.md) for volume, fades, ducking, mute and solo, which all affect what Remove Silences hears, and [MCP](mcp.md) for the full tool reference.

# Captions and transcription

Frame Job brings captions in from a SubRip file, writes them from the speech in your clips, and writes a caption track back out as `.srt` or `.vtt`. Speech is recognised either **on this Mac**, with nothing uploaded, or by **AssemblyAI** in the cloud, using your own API key. Captions come out as two-line subtitles or as large word-by-word captions in one of five styles, where each word lights up as it is said. Every caption is an ordinary text clip, so it plays in the preview, burns into an export, and can be dragged, trimmed and restyled like any other clip.

All three commands are in the **File** menu, next to each other:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| **File ▸ Import Captions…** | Reads a SubRip (`.srt`) file onto a new caption track. |
| **File ▸ Generate Captions…** | Transcribes the speech in your clips onto a new caption track. |
| **File ▸ Export Captions…** | Writes one caption track out as SubRip (`.srt`) or WebVTT (`.vtt`). |

None of the three has a keyboard shortcut.

## Captions are text clips

However a caption gets onto the timeline, it ends up as a text clip on a track of its own at the front of the stack, so it draws over everything else. That has some useful effects:

- The preview, a rendered frame and an exported movie all show it. Burn-in needs no extra step.
- You can drag one to retime it, trim its edges, split it or delete it with the usual tools ([Editing](editing.md)).
- You can select a run of captions and restyle them together in the inspector's Clip tab, under **Text** ([Canvas and layers](canvas-and-layers.md)).
- Captions are not a soft-subtitle track that a player can switch on and off. To ship a separate subtitle file, use **Export Captions…**.

The first caption track is named **Captions**, then **Captions 2**, **Captions 3** and so on, so separate runs can be told apart in the track headers.
