Both are greyed out while the sheet cannot work out a valid file, for example when a custom field is empty. The readout then says what to fix.

The save panel suggests the project's name with the format's extension (`Board v1.2.mp4`). It says what is being written: "Export the timeline as a movie.", "Export the timeline as an animated GIF." or "Export the timeline's audio."

### The progress sheet

**Exporting** shows a progress bar and a percentage. The status line reads "Preparing “*name*”…", then "Measuring loudness…" while the sound is measured, then "Writing “*name*”…".

- **Cancel** stops the export ("Stopping…") and removes the half-written file.
- When it finishes, the line reads "Exported “*name*”." followed by what the sound measured, for example `Peak −1.0 dBTP · −14.0 LUFS`. **Show in Finder** reveals the file, and **Close** dismisses the sheet.
- If a graphic warned while the file was drawn, the line adds a count ("1 graphic warning"), and the tooltip lists each warning with its frame.
- A failure shows its reason on the sheet, and **Close** dismisses it.

### What the loudness line means

| Line | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Peak −1.0 dBTP · −14.0 LUFS` | The true peak and integrated loudness of the file. |
| `Peak … · loudness not measurable` | The sound is too short or too quiet to have a loudness. |
| `Silent` | The sound is digital silence. |
| `… · peaks limited by 8.6 dB` | The master limiter turned the loudest peak down by that much to hold the ceiling. A large figure on music can be audible; turn the clips down, or ask for a lower target. |

## The Export Queue

**Window ▸ Export Queue** lists queued exports. It opens on its own whenever you click **Add to Queue**.

- Jobs run **one at a time**, in the order they were added, while you keep editing.
- An **AV1** or **VP9** job also waits for memory. These formats are encoded in software and use a lot of it: about 1.2–2.4 GB at 1080p and 4.4–8.1 GB at 4K for AV1, depending on Speed, and about 0.4–0.5 GB at 1080p and 1.1–1.6 GB at 4K for VP9. All AV1 and VP9 exports running in Frame Job at once, from the queue and from **Export…** progress sheets, may use up to a quarter of the Mac's memory together. A queued AV1 or VP9 job that would go over waits until enough of them finish, and its row says why. The row's status is one line and ends in "…" where the sentence does not fit, which at most window widths is before the figures; hold the pointer over the row and its tooltip ends with the whole sentence: "Waiting for memory: AV1 and VP9 exports running now hold about 2.3 GB of the 4.0 GB this Mac allows them, and this one needs about 2.2 GB." While it waits, a later job that fits runs first. When nothing else is running, a job always starts, however large. An **Export…** sheet never waits: it is counted, and starts straight away.
- A job holds the timeline **as it was when you confirmed it**, including its media files, reversed clips and graphics. Edits, undos, relinks and even closing the document afterwards do not change what it writes.
- Each row shows the file's name and its state: **Waiting** (or the memory wait above), *Writing · 42 %* (or the measuring phase), the "Exported …" line with its loudness figures, **Cancelled.**, **Cancelled before it started.**, or the reason a job failed. The tooltip shows the full path, the format, size and frame rate, the whole memory-wait sentence while a job waits for memory, and any graphic warnings.
- **Cancel** on a row stops that job and removes its half-written file. On a finished row the button reads **Remove** and takes the row out of the list. **Show** reveals a finished file in the Finder.
- If a later export writes to the same file, the earlier finished row reads "Overwritten by a later export to the same file."
- **Clear Finished** removes every finished, cancelled and failed row. **Cancel All** stops the running job and every waiting one.
- The line at the bottom, beside **Clear Finished** and **Cancel All**, counts the jobs: "1 exporting · 2 waiting · 3 finished".
- With nothing queued, the window says so: "Nothing queued. The Export card's Add to Queue button puts a confirmed export here instead of waiting for it, and they run one at a time while you keep editing."

Closing the window stops nothing. Opening the export sheet pauses playback whichever button you use, but after **Add to Queue** there is no progress sheet in the way: you can resume playback and keep editing while the job runs.

Quitting while a queued job runs or waits asks first: "An export is still being written." The message names the running file and counts the jobs still waiting ("“*name*” is not finished, and 2 more are waiting."). **Quit Anyway** cancels the queue and deletes the partly written file. This question comes after Frame Job has asked about unsaved documents.

Only queued exports are protected this way. Quitting while an **Export…** progress sheet is writing does not ask, and the half-written file is left behind. Cancel that export first.

## Saving a single frame

**File ▸ Save Frame…** (⌥⌘E) saves the frame under the playhead as a still. The save panel suggests the project's name and the timecode, with `-` for `:` (`Board 00-00-12-05.png`). Its **Format** popup offers:

| Format | Alpha | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **PNG** | Kept | The default. |
| **JPEG** | None | A transparent canvas is flattened onto black. |
| **HEIC** | Kept | |

- The **Format** popup opens on PNG every time. It does not remember your last choice.
- Under the popup, a line says what the chosen format does with transparency: "PNG keeps the canvas's alpha channel." or "JPEG has no alpha channel: a transparent canvas is flattened onto black."
- Choosing a format changes the file name's extension in the panel. A name you typed is kept.
- JPEG and HEIC are written at 90 % quality.

- The frame is drawn the way an export draws it, at the canvas's full size. Preview Quality, Show Ungraded and Show SDR Version never change it. There is no timecode burn-in.
- Inside a nest, the frame is the nest's own picture at the nest's time.
- A frame showing a deep still or a 10-bit VP9 clip is saved as a 16-bit PNG or 10-bit HEIC. JPEG is always 8-bit.
- In an HDR (HLG) project, PNG and HEIC keep the HLG picture and a JPEG is the SDR version (see [HDR and colour](hdr-and-color.md)).
- When there is no frame at the playhead, an alert says so.
- If the file cannot be written, an alert says why: the folder is missing or Frame Job cannot write into it, or this Mac has no encoder for the format.

Save Frame… is greyed out while the timeline is empty.

*Agents:* `render_frame` writes the same file for the same frame (see [For agents](#for-agents)).

## HDR projects

In an HDR (HLG) project the sheet has a **Dynamic Range** row under Format:

| Choice | What the file holds |
|---|---|
| **HDR (HLG)** | The HLG master. The default. |
| **HDR10 (PQ)** | An HDR10 file with fixed mastering metadata. |
| **SDR version** | The project converted to SDR. |

Only HEVC 10-bit, both AV1 formats, VP9 (WebM), ProRes 422 and ProRes 4444 can carry HDR (VP9 with Alpha (WebM) is always 8-bit and writes the SDR version). VP9 (WebM) is 10-bit (VP9 Profile 2) for HLG and HDR10, and 8-bit (Profile 0, which every player decodes) for the SDR version. On every other video format the row is greyed out on **SDR version**, which is what those formats write. What each choice contains, and how the SDR version is made, is in [HDR and colour](hdr-and-color.md#exporting-hdr).

## Transparency

A canvas whose background is transparent (the **Background** row in the Document tab's Appearance section; see [Projects and media](projects-and-media.md#appearance)) keeps its transparency only in **ProRes 4444**, **HEVC with Alpha**, **VP9 with Alpha (WebM)** and **Animated PNG**. When the format carries an alpha channel, the footnote ends in "alpha". Every other format composites the picture onto black. A GIF can show a pixel as fully transparent but has no partial transparency, so it is not one of the four.

Which transparent movie to send:

- **VP9 with Alpha (WebM)** plays with its transparency in Chrome and Firefox, in a web page's `<video>`. Safari has not been confirmed to show it (see Limits). Only a player that decodes VP9 with the libvpx decoder shows the transparency; others, ffmpeg's default decoder among them, show the picture opaque.
- **HEVC with Alpha** is the transparent movie for Safari, QuickTime and Apple's apps.
- **ProRes 4444** is the master for another editor.

The colour in all three is straight, not multiplied by the transparency, so a re-imported file composites to the right colour.

While the canvas background is transparent, the Document tab says how many formats will keep it: "Transparent — kept by 4 export formats." These are the four formats above.

## Chapters

Chapter markers on the timeline (see [Timeline](timeline.md)) become chapters in MP4, MOV, M4A and WebM files, in time order. A chapter's name is the marker's name, or "Chapter *n*" for an unnamed one. A range export keeps the chapters inside the range, with their times counted from the start of the file, and the chapter already running when the range starts opens the file. WAV, AIFF, GIF and APNG have no chapters.

MP4 and M4A files are written with their index at the front, so a player can start before the whole file has downloaded.

## What an export includes

- **The same picture and sound as the preview.** The export uses the same composition and the same compositor. View-only settings never reach it: Preview Quality, Show Ungraded, Show SDR Version, Show Selection, safe areas and the scopes.
- **Speed ramps and Keep pitch off.** An export waits for the rendered audio of every speed ramp, and of every clip at a constant speed other than ×1 with Keep pitch off, to finish before it writes, and shows "Preparing…" meanwhile. That sound is never exported silent (see [Speed](speed.md)). If it cannot be rendered, the export fails with "Clip *n*'s retimed audio could not be rendered: …".
- **The gate, the leveller and the de-esser.** Their thresholds follow each clip's measured loudness, and the leveller works from the clip's speech too, so an export waits, showing "Preparing…", until every gated, levelled or de-essed clip in it has been measured. If a measurement has not landed after five minutes, the export fails with "Clip *n*'s loudness or speech has not been measured yet, so its gate, leveller and de-esser cannot be set. Wait for their Status rows to show the clip's loudness, then export again." (see [Audio](audio.md#gate)).
- **Missing media.** A clip whose file is missing still exports, showing its slate and with no sound. An audio track none of whose clips can be read is written as silence instead of failing the export.
- **Graphics.** An export draws the graphics as they were when it was asked for, even if a module is saved again mid-export. If a graphic in the range, or in a nest the range reaches, does not compile or has no module, the export does not start and names the graphic. If a graphic fails while the file is being written, the export stops at that frame, names the graphic, and leaves no file. See [Graphics](graphics.md).
- **Captions** are ordinary text clips, so they are always burned into the picture. To write a separate subtitle file, use **File ▸ Export Captions…** (see [Captions](captions.md)).

## For agents

`export` mirrors **Export…** with **Add to Queue**: it checks the request, puts the job in the Export Queue and answers at once with `{export_id, path, status}`. Status is `queued` or `running`.

| Argument | The sheet's control | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `preset` (required) | Format | `h264`, `hevc`, `hevc_alpha`, `hevc_10bit`, `av1`, `av1_webm`, `vp9_webm`, `vp9_alpha_webm`, `prores_422`, `prores_4444`, `audio_m4a`, `audio_wav`, `audio_aiff`, `gif`, `apng`. |
| `path` (required) | Save panel | The folder must exist. An existing file is replaced. The format's extension is added when the path has none, and a different known media extension is replaced: `cut.mov` with `h264` writes `cut.mp4`. Any other suffix stays part of the name. |
| `size` | Size | `document`, `2160p`, `1440p`, `1080p`, `720p`, `preset` (GIF and APNG only), or `[width, height]`. |
| `range` | Range | `project` (default) or `in_out`. Refused when there is no in/out range. |
| `video_bitrate`, `audio_bitrate` | Quality | Bits per second. On `av1`, `av1_webm` and `vp9_webm`, `video_bitrate` is a soft cap the file usually stays under. On `vp9_alpha_webm` it is the same soft cap on the picture's stream alone, and the transparency's stream comes on top of it (about 6–15 % of the video at 1080p, up to about 39 % at 640 × 360, measured). `audio_bitrate` is the AAC or Opus rate. |
| `loudness_lufs` | Loudness | −70 to 0. |
| `peak_dbtp` | (fixed at −1 on the sheet) | −20 to 0: the master limiter's ceiling, −1 when absent. Legal with or without `loudness_lufs`. |
| `audio_bits` | Bit depth | `16` (default) or `24`. `audio_wav` and `audio_aiff` only; refused on every other format. |
| `stems` | Stems | `tracks` or `names`. `audio_m4a`, `audio_wav` and `audio_aiff` only; refused on every other format and when no track can be heard. See [Stems](#stems). |
| `burn_in_timecode` | Burn in timecode | |
| `dynamic_range` | Dynamic Range | `hlg`, `pq` or `sdr`. |
| `encoder_speed` | Speed | `faster`, `balanced` (default) or `smaller`. `av1` and `av1_webm` only; refused on every other format, `vp9_webm` and `vp9_alpha_webm` included. |

There is no frame-rate argument. An agent's export uses the document's rate, or GIF's and APNG's own.

Every refusal comes back from `export` itself, before anything is queued: a bad argument, a missing folder, an empty timeline, or a graphic that does not compile.

- `export_status {export_id}` answers the job's row without waiting: `queued`, `running` (with `progress` from 0 to 1 and `phase`), `done`, `failed` or `cancelled`. Call it again after a pause until the job finishes.
  - Every answer has `path` and `elapsed` (seconds).
  - `done` adds `bytes`, the settings the file was written with, `burn_in_timecode`, `dynamic_range` in an HLG project, `encoder_speed` for AV1 and AV1 (WebM), `audio_bits` for WAV and AIFF, `stems` (`[{name, tracks, path}]`, each file beside the mix) when stems were asked, any `graphic_warnings` and, for every format with sound, `loudness`: `summary`, `integrated_lufs`, `true_peak_dbtp`, `sample_peak_dbfs`, `gain_db`, `ceiling_dbtp` (the master limiter's), `limited_db` (how far it turned the loudest peak down), `capped_by_gain` (the 40 dB limit decided the gain) and `target_lufs`.
  - `queued` adds `waiting`, the row's "Waiting for memory: …" sentence, while an AV1 or VP9 job waits for memory.
  - `queued` and `running` add `estimated_seconds` for `av1`, `av1_webm`, `vp9_webm` and `vp9_alpha_webm`: the export sheet's estimate of the whole export, in whole seconds.
  - `failed` and `cancelled` add `reason`, the queue row's sentence.
- `cancel_export {export_id}` is the row's Cancel.
- An `export_id` lasts until Frame Job quits.
- `render_frame` renders one frame through the same path as Save Frame…. It returns the image inline and as a file, and with no `path` it writes a temporary PNG and names it. An explicit `format` wins and replaces the path's extension, so `{path: "shot.jpg", format: "png"}` writes `shot.png`. When a graphic in the frame warned or failed, the reply names it, its frame and the message, and a failed graphic draws its error card in the picture. It takes `t` (default: the playhead), `path`, `format` (`png`, `jpeg`, `heic`), `max_width` and `burn_in_timecode`, plus `sdr_version`, `ungraded`, `selection` and the scope measurements described in [Colour grading](color-grading.md) and [HDR and colour](hdr-and-color.md).

The full reference is [MCP](mcp.md).

## Limits

- An animated GIF or APNG holds at most **600 frames**: 48 seconds at GIF's 12.5 fps, or 24 seconds at APNG's 25 fps. A longer range is refused. Shorten the range or lower the frame rate.
- A loudness target more than 40 dB above the mix lands quieter than asked, and the report's `capped_by_gain` says so.
- The master limiter cannot be turned off; 0 dBTP is its loosest ceiling. The preview has no master limiter, so a mix that passes −1 dBTP sounds louder while editing than in the file.
- ProRes 4444, HEVC with Alpha and VP9 with Alpha (WebM) refuse a custom size of a different shape from the canvas.
- VP9 with Alpha (WebM) is 8-bit SDR only: an HDR project writes its SDR version, and HDR is refused on it.
- A VP9 with Alpha (WebM) file re-imported into Frame Job keeps its picture and loses its transparency: it shows opaque, with black where it was transparent. Export ProRes 4444 or HEVC with Alpha for a transparent clip to bring back in.
- Whether Safari shows VP9 with Alpha (WebM)'s transparency has not been confirmed; use HEVC with Alpha for Safari.
- A Mac with no encoder for a format reports "This Mac cannot export with the “*preset*” preset." and leaves no file.
- 24-bit is offered on WAV and AIFF only. ProRes, AAC and Opus sound is 16-bit, and nothing is dithered.
- On an M1 or M2 Mac Frame Job cannot play or re-import its own AV1 file, MP4 or WebM; QuickTime cannot either. Those Macs have no AV1 decoder. A VP9 (WebM) file re-imports on any Apple silicon Mac.
- AV1's and VP9's file size is not known in advance: the file usually comes in well under the rate, but very detailed footage can go up to about 1.25 times over it with AV1 and about 1.15 times with VP9.
- Captions are burned in, never a switchable subtitle track.
- Queued jobs run one at a time. **Export…** does not join the queue: it writes straight away, behind its own progress sheet.
- A queued AV1 or VP9 job waits while the AV1 and VP9 exports already running would use more than a quarter of the Mac's memory with it. The memory each needs is a measured figure, not a guarantee: a heavier timeline can use more. An **Export…** sheet is never held, so starting several AV1 or VP9 sheets at once can go past that quarter.
- The estimated time is the median of three measured exports per format and size, of real 4K camera footage on one idle Mac (an Apple M2 Max). On exports it was not fitted on, 30 seconds at 2560 × 1440, it came within 14 % of the real time; a slower Mac, a busy one or a heavier timeline takes longer.
- Quitting during an **Export…** progress-sheet export does not ask and leaves a half-written file. Only the Export Queue is guarded at quit.

# Exporting

Frame Job writes the timeline out as a movie, an audio file or an animated image, and saves single frames as stills. One export sheet covers every format. You choose the format, then the size, frame rate, quality, loudness and range, and the sheet shows what the file will be before anything is written. Exports can run at once behind a progress sheet, or wait in the Export Queue while you keep editing. Every export of a file with sound reports what that sound measured.

## Opening the export sheet

Choose **File ▸ Export…** (⌘E), or click **Export…** at the right end of the toolbar. Playback pauses and the sheet opens over the editor window.

The command is greyed out while the timeline is empty. An export always writes the whole top-level timeline, even when you are working inside a nest.

The sheet reopens on the **last choices you exported with**. Clicking **Export…** or **Add to Queue** records them; Cancel does not. With nothing remembered, it opens on H.264 at the document's own size.

The remembered choice belongs to the app, not to the project, so every document's sheet opens on it. A remembered **In/out range** falls back to **Whole project** on a document that has no range.

## The controls

From top to bottom:

| Control | What it does | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Preset** | Applies a saved set of choices (see [Presets](#presets)). The gear beside it saves and deletes presets. | Custom |
| **Format** | The encoding: container and codec together. | H.264 (MP4) |
| **Dynamic Range** | Shown only in an HDR (HLG) project. See [HDR projects](#hdr-projects). | HDR (HLG) |
| **Speed** | How long the AV1 encoder works on each frame. See [Speed](#speed). | Balanced |
| **Size** | The frame size, or **Custom…** with width and height fields on the row below. | The format's first row |
| **Frame rate** | **Project rate**, or a fixed rate. | Project rate |
| **Quality** | **Format default**, or a bit-rate tier. | Format default |
| **Bit depth** | **16-bit** or **24-bit**, for WAV and AIFF. See [Bit depth](#bit-depth). | 16-bit |
| **Stems** | **None**, **One per Track** or **One per Track Name**: also write each track's sound as its own file, for the audio formats. See [Stems](#stems). | None |
| **Loudness** | **Off**, a loudness target, or **Custom…** with a LUFS field. | Off |
| **Range** | **Whole project**, or **In/out range** when one is set. | Whole project |
| **Burn in timecode** | Draws the project timecode into the picture. | Off |

Under the controls, a readout line describes the file and a footnote names the codec, the container and the rates the file will use. Every number they show is the size, rate and duration the file will actually have.

- **Readout:** `1920 × 1080 · 30 fps · 00:01:12:05` (size, frame rate, duration). For the audio-only formats it reads `Audio only · 00:01:12.200`. For GIF and APNG it adds the frame count: `· 360 frames, no audio`. For **AV1 (MP4)**, **AV1 (WebM)**, **VP9 (WebM)** and **VP9 with Alpha (WebM)** a second line estimates how long the export will take: `Estimated time: about 25 s` (in 5-second steps under a minute, then minutes, then hours and minutes). It follows the format, Speed, size and range, and it is only an estimate: the figures behind it are the median of three measured exports per format at 1080p and 4K, of real 4K camera footage on an idle Apple M2 Max, so a slower or busy Mac, or a heavy timeline, takes longer. The other formats show no estimate.
- **Footnote:** the codec, the container (left out when it is the same word, as in `GIF`), the AV1 speed (`AV1 · MP4 · Balanced`, `AV1 · WEBM · Balanced`; VP9 has none: `VP9 · WEBM`, `VP9 · WEBM · alpha`), the video rate, the audio rate (`192 kbps audio`), `24-bit` for a 24-bit WAV or AIFF, the loudness target (`−14 LUFS`) and `alpha` when the format keeps transparency. When you pick a Quality tier and the format sets its own rate, it reads `format's own rate` instead of a number.

A control the chosen format cannot use is greyed out rather than hidden. Its value is not sent.

### Format

| Format | Container | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| H.264 (MP4) | `.mp4` | The everyday delivery file. 8-bit. |
| HEVC (MP4) | `.mp4` | A smaller file at the same picture. 8-bit (Main profile). |
| HEVC with Alpha (MOV) | `.mov` | A small delivery file that keeps a transparent canvas, for laying over another background. 8-bit. |
| HEVC 10-bit (MP4) | `.mp4` | Keeps a 10-bit source's gradients (Main 10). |
| AV1 (MP4) | `.mp4` | The smallest delivery file, encoded by the AV1 encoder built into Frame Job. 10-bit, and it can carry HDR. Slower to export than HEVC. See [Speed](#speed). |
| AV1 (WebM) | `.webm` | The same AV1 picture in a WebM file, with Opus sound, for the web. Frame Job writes the WebM itself. |
| VP9 (WebM) | `.webm` | VP9 in a WebM file, with Opus sound: the web format every browser plays, encoded by the VP9 encoder built into Frame Job. 8-bit, or 10-bit when it carries HDR. Slower to export than HEVC and larger than AV1 for the same picture. |
| VP9 with Alpha (WebM) | `.webm` | VP9 (WebM) that keeps a transparent canvas, for a title or a lower third a web page plays over its own background in Chrome or Firefox. 8-bit, always the SDR picture. Safari's transparent movie is HEVC with Alpha. |
| ProRes 422 (MOV) | `.mov` | An editing master for another application. 10-bit. |
| ProRes 4444 (MOV) | `.mov` | A master that keeps the alpha channel. 12-bit. |
| Audio only (M4A) | `.m4a` | AAC sound only. |
| Audio only (WAV) | `.wav` | Uncompressed 16-bit or 24-bit, 48 kHz sound. |
| Audio only (AIFF) | `.aiff` | The same samples as WAV, in an AIFF file. |
| Animated GIF | `.gif` | A short silent loop. Capped at 480 × 270 and 12.5 fps by default. |
| Animated PNG | `.png` | A lossless silent loop with real transparency. Capped at 960 × 540 and 25 fps by default. |

Sound in the movie formats is stereo at 48 kHz: AAC in H.264, HEVC, HEVC with Alpha and AV1 (MP4), Opus in AV1 (WebM) and both VP9 formats, and 16-bit LPCM in both ProRes formats. A project with no sound exports a WebM with no sound track. GIF and APNG carry no sound. A file's sound is exactly as long as the range it exports, including when a clip in it plays faster or slower.

Changing the format rebuilds the Size list and puts it back on that format's default. Your frame rate, quality, loudness and range choices stay as they were.

### Size

The Size popup lists, in order:

- **GIF default** or **APNG default**: the format's cap. Only on those two formats, and it is their default.
- **Document size**: the canvas as it is. On a format that needs even dimensions and a canvas with an odd edge, this row is named **Document (even)** and is one pixel smaller on that edge.
- **4K**, **1440p**, **1080p**, **720p**: the number is the short edge. The long edge follows the document's shape, rounded to an even number, so a vertical project's 1080p is 1080 × 1920.
- **Custom…**: type a width and a height, each from 16 to 8192 pixels. The fields start from the size that was chosen a moment before.

A row with the same numbers as an earlier row is hidden, so a 1920 × 1080 document shows Document size and no separate 1080p. Sizes larger than the document are offered, so a 720p recording can be exported at 4K.

How the picture fits the frame:

- **Even dimensions.** H.264, HEVC, HEVC with Alpha, HEVC 10-bit, both AV1 formats, both VP9 formats and ProRes 422 need them, so an odd width or height is written one pixel smaller. ProRes 4444, GIF and APNG keep an odd edge.
- **Movies** are written at exactly the size you choose. When that size is within a pixel of the canvas's shape, the picture fills the frame edge to edge. Any other shape is letterboxed with black.
- **ProRes 4444, HEVC with Alpha and VP9 with Alpha (WebM)** refuse a size of a different shape instead of letterboxing it, because the padding would destroy the alpha channel. Every row in the Size popup has the canvas's shape, so this only happens with a Custom size.
- **GIF and APNG** fit the picture inside the size you choose, keeping its shape and never enlarging it. The readout shows the size the file will have: a 1080 × 1920 project's GIF default is 152 × 270.

The Size control is greyed out for the audio-only formats.

### Speed

The **Speed** row sits under Format (under Dynamic Range in an HDR project). It is live only on **AV1 (MP4)** and **AV1 (WebM)**; on every other format it is greyed out and keeps your last choice. **VP9 (WebM)** and **VP9 with Alpha (WebM)** have one speed, so the row is greyed out there too.

| Choice | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Faster** | The quickest AV1 export and the largest file. On 10 seconds of 4K camera footage it took about half Balanced's time (7.1 s against 14.0 s on an Apple M2 Max) and wrote a file 27 % larger; at 1080p 2.4 s against 4.2 s, 4 % larger. |
| **Balanced** | The default. |
| **Smaller file** | The slowest AV1 export and the smallest file. On the same footage it took about 1.4 times Balanced's time (19.9 s against 14.0 s at 4K, 5.8 s against 4.2 s at 1080p) and wrote a file 12 % smaller at 4K, 5 % smaller at 1080p. |

AV1 and VP9 are encoded in software, so they take longer than the HEVC formats, which use the Mac's hardware encoder. The choice is remembered with the rest of the sheet and stored in presets.

### Frame rate

**Project rate** exports at the document's frame rate, or at the format's own rate for GIF (12.5 fps) and APNG (25 fps). The fixed choices are 24, 23.976, 25, 30, 29.97, 50 and 60 fps. Greyed out for the audio-only formats.

### Quality

**Format default** lets the encoder choose the video rate. The sound uses 192 kbps AAC, or 192 kbps Opus in the two WebM formats.

The four tiers set a video rate from the frame's size, so a tier means the same picture quality at every size. Each tier's title shows the rate it would ask for at the size and frame rate now chosen.

| Tier | Video at 1080p, 30 fps or less (H.264) | AAC sound |
|---|---|---|
| **Low** | 4.0 Mbps | 128 kbps |
| **Medium** | 6.0 Mbps | 192 kbps |
| **High** | 8.0 Mbps | 256 kbps |
| **Maximum** | 12.0 Mbps | 320 kbps |

- The video rate scales with the frame's area. High is about 3.6 Mbps at 720p and 32 Mbps at 4K.
- Above 30 fps, the video rate is 1.5 times higher.
- HEVC formats, AV1 and VP9 ask for 60 % of the H.264 rate. AV1's and VP9's **Format default** is the HEVC rate too.
- For **AV1** the rate is a soft cap. AV1 encodes at a constant quality chosen to match or beat HEVC at that rate, so it usually stays under the rate and simple footage comes out much smaller. Very detailed footage can go over: up to about 1.25 times the rate was measured. Its tier titles and footnote read `usually ≤ …`.
- For **VP9 (WebM)** the rate is a soft cap the same way: VP9 encodes at a constant quality chosen to match or beat HEVC at that rate (HEVC 10-bit's in an HDR export), and the file usually stays under it. Up to about 1.15 times the rate was measured. Its tier titles and footnote read `usually ≤ …` too. On **VP9 with Alpha (WebM)** the rate is the picture's alone: the transparency is a second stream at a fixed quality that comes on top of it, so the file is larger than the rate says. In the measured exports of a moving soft-edged shape the transparency was about 6–15 % of the video at 1080p, about 9–21 % at 720p and about 21–39 % at 640 × 360 (the higher figure at the Low tier); a smaller picture keeps its edges clean with a larger share.
- The WebM formats ask the same rates of their Opus sound, rounded to the nearest rate the Opus encoder offers.
- Audio only (M4A) uses the tier's AAC rate alone.
- Quality is greyed out for ProRes, WAV, AIFF, GIF and APNG, where the format fixes the rate.

### Bit depth

The **Bit depth** row sits under Quality. It is live only on **Audio only (WAV)** and **Audio only (AIFF)**; on every other format it is greyed out and keeps your last choice. **16-bit** is the default; **24-bit** keeps detail 16-bit cannot, which matters most for a quiet recording you are going to raise or process later. Both are rounded once from the mix, never dithered. ProRes's sound stays 16-bit. The choice is remembered with the rest of the sheet and stored in presets.

### Stems

The **Stems** row sits under Bit depth. It is live only on **Audio only (M4A)**, **Audio only (WAV)** and **Audio only (AIFF)**; on every other format it is greyed out and keeps your last choice. With a choice other than **None**, the export writes the mix and, beside it, one file per stem, in the same format, for mixing or mastering in another editor.

- **One per Track** writes one stem for each track you can hear.
- **One per Track Name** writes one stem for each track name: tracks whose names match, ignoring case and spaces at either end, share one file, named the way the first of them is spelled. A track with no name gets its own.
- A muted track has no stem, and while any track is soloed only the soloed tracks have one. A track with no sound on it (only pictures, or nothing) has none. If no track can be heard, the export is refused: "stems: no track is heard, so there is no stem to write".
- A stem is named after the mix and its track: exporting `Mix.wav` writes `Mix - Dialogue.wav` and `Mix - Music.wav`. A track with no name is called by its header's label, `Track 3`. A `/` or `:` in a track name is written as `-`, and a second stem whose name an earlier one already has, ignoring case, gets its track's label after it: `vo (Track 2)`. If an earlier stem already has that name too, a count follows the label, `vo (Track 2, 2)`, so no two stems share a file.
- **An existing file at a stem's name is replaced without asking.** The save panel asks only about the mix. The one exception: if a stem's file would be one of the project's own media files, the export stops before writing any stem, with "The stem “Mix - Dialogue.wav” would replace media this project uses; export under another name."
- Each stem holds its tracks' sound exactly as the mix plays it, with the clips' and tracks' volume, pan, fades, ducking and effects, and a track's own compressor and limiter, but **before the master**: no loudness target is applied to it and the master limiter does not touch it. So the stems added together are the mix, to within the last bit, wherever the master neither raised the level nor limited a peak. A stem can therefore peak higher than the mix; it is clipped only at full scale.
- The stems are written one after another after the mix, and the progress bar counts them. The finish line reads "Exported “Mix.wav” and 3 stems.", and the footnote under the sheet says "3 stems". The loudness figures are the mix's. Cancelling, or a failure part-way, removes the mix and every stem already written.

### Loudness

Loudness normalises the whole mix to an integrated loudness target, measured to ITU-R BS.1770-4.

| Choice | Target |
|---|---|
| **Off** | No normalisation. The export still measures its sound and reports it. |
| **−14 LUFS (streaming)** | Where the main streaming services normalise. |
| **−16 LUFS** | The usual target for stereo podcasts. |
| **−23 LUFS (broadcast)** | EBU R 128 broadcast delivery. |
| **Custom…** | Type any target from −70 to 0 LUFS, to one decimal place. |

How normalisation works:

- The export measures the real mix first. The progress line reads "Measuring loudness…" during this pass.
- It then applies **one gain** to everything. Levels inside the timeline keep their relationship to each other.
- The gain is worked out through the export's master limiter (below), so the file lands on the target even when its loudest peaks would pass the ceiling: those peaks are turned down instead of the whole mix. Only a target more than 40 dB above the mix falls short.

**Every export with sound goes through a master limiter**, normalised or not. It keeps the file's true peak under **−1 dBTP**: a mix that would pass that, from loud clips, a crossfade between two loud clips, a nest turned up or an action that raises a clip's volume, is limited instead of clipped. Sound under the ceiling passes through untouched, sample for sample. The limiter looks 3.3 ms ahead, and the export takes that back, so the sound stays exactly in sync with the picture. The preview has no master limiter: what you hear while editing is the mix before it.

A track's own compressor and limiter ([Audio](audio.md#track-compressor-and-limiter)) run before the master, on that track's sound alone, exactly as set: the export plays each such track on its own through them and mixes the tracks afterwards. The measurement for a loudness target hears them too, so the file still lands on the target. The master is only the loudness gain and this limiter; there is no master compressor or EQ. To compress the whole mix, nest everything onto one track and give that track a compressor.

The sheet fixes the ceiling at −1 dBTP. An agent can choose another (see [For agents](#for-agents)). Loudness is greyed out for GIF and APNG.

For per-clip levels, fades and Normalize, see [Audio](audio.md).

### Range

**Whole project** writes the whole timeline. **In/out range** writes only the range set on the timeline (see [Timeline](timeline.md)), snapped to the export's frame grid. The popup is greyed out when there is no range.

Inside a nest, the popup is greyed out even when the nest has a range, and its tooltip says why: an export writes the whole timeline, so it cannot use a range that belongs to the nest. Leave the nest (⌘↑) and set the range on the timeline.

### Burn in timecode

**Burn in timecode** writes the project's timecode into the exported picture, centred near the bottom and on top of everything, including captions. It appears only in the exported file, never in the preview.

- It uses the document's own timecode format, `HH:MM:SS:FF` or `HH:MM:SS.mmm`, non-drop, as the toolbar shows it.
- It shows **project time**. A file exported from an in/out range that starts at 00:00:10:00 begins at 00:00, but its first frame reads 00:00:10:00. That is the number a reviewer's note needs.

Greyed out for the audio-only formats.

## Presets

A preset stores the **choices** on the card: the format, size row or custom size, frame rate, quality tier, loudness, range and burn-in. It does not store the numbers they resolve to. A preset saved on a 1080p document that says "4K, High" exports at the right 4K size and rate on any other document.

- **Apply a preset:** pick it from the **Preset** popup. Every control is set exactly as if you had clicked it.
- **Save a preset:** click the gear and choose **Save…**, type a name and click **Save**. The name field starts with the name of the preset now chosen. Saving under a name that already exists (ignoring case) replaces that preset. The name "Custom" is reserved. While the card has an error, for example an empty custom field, **Save…** beeps and saves nothing.
- **Delete a preset:** choose it in the popup, then choose **Delete** from the gear. Delete is available only while a saved preset is chosen, and it asks no confirmation. The controls keep the preset's values, so **Save…** under the same name puts it back.
- **Change a preset:** apply it, adjust the controls, and save again under the same name. There is no separate rename.

Changing any control by hand puts the popup back on **Custom**. The popup also opens on Custom each time, even when the remembered choices happen to match a preset.

Presets are kept for your whole account in `~/Library/Application Support/Frame Job/ExportPresets.json`, so every project and window shares them. The **Dynamic Range** choice is not stored in a preset or in the remembered choices.

## Writing the file

The sheet has three buttons:

- **Cancel** closes the sheet. Nothing is written and nothing is remembered.
- **Export…** opens a save panel, then writes the file behind a progress sheet.
- **Add to Queue** opens the same save panel, then puts the job in the Export Queue so you can keep editing.

# Motion graphics

A graphic clip is a motion graphic drawn fresh on every frame by a small
JavaScript module kept inside your project. Frame Job ships twenty-three
ready-made graphics (charts, a gauge and timers, screencast keys and window
frames, title, quote and logo cards, and social pop-ups), and you can bring in
your own module or have an agent write one. Each module declares the
properties it takes, and the inspector turns those into controls, so you can
change text, colours and numbers without touching code, and animate them over
time like any other clip property.

The language a module is written in (the `render` function, `ctx`, the schema,
the standard library, fonts, the sandbox and its limits) is documented in the
[graphics API reference](../graphics-api.md). This page covers using graphics
in the editor.

## What a graphic is

- A **module** is one file, `graphics/<name>.js`, in the project's package. It
  draws an SVG picture for any frame you ask for. The same frame always draws
  the same picture: a module cannot reach the network, the clock or random
  numbers other than its own seeded ones.
- A **graphic clip** is a clip on the timeline drawn by a module. It names the
  module, the size the module draws at, the graphic's own timeline, and the
  property values to draw with. Many clips can share one module, each with
  its own values.
- A module's **properties** (its schema) are typed: number, boolean, colour,
  menu (enum), text, or picture (asset). A value you don't set draws with the
  module's own default.
- **Gradients don't band.** Where a gradient is rounded to the 256 levels a
  graphic is drawn in, Frame Job adds a fixed, fine pattern under half a
  level, so a dark gradient shades smoothly instead of in steps. Flat
  colours, pictures, text and transparency are drawn exactly. The pattern
  survives `render_frame`, Save Frame… and ProRes. A 10-bit export
  (`hevc_10bit`) smooths most of it away but keeps the in-between shades,
  so the gradient stays smooth; an 8-bit H.264 or HEVC export smooths it
  away too, and its steps come back.

Module names use lowercase letters, digits and `-`, start with a letter or a
digit, and are at most 63 characters (`lower-third`, `title-2`).

Graphics draw only with the fonts bundled with Frame Job and the ones you add
to the project (see [Fonts and pictures](#fonts-and-pictures)), never with
the fonts installed on your Mac, so a project draws the same everywhere.

## Adding a graphic

**Insert ▸ Graphic…** opens the Graphic dialog. On the left are the
categories: **This Project** first, when the project's `graphics/` folder
holds a module (every module in it, whatever its own category), then the
bundled templates' categories, in alphabetical order. In the middle are the
chosen category's graphics, by name. On the right a preview plays the chosen
graphic over a checkerboard, looping, at the project's canvas shape, with its
name and a one-line description under it. A module that doesn't compile is
listed in grey and its preview is the red error card.

The dialog opens on the first category's first graphic. **Insert** (Return,
or a double-click on a graphic) adds the chosen graphic; **Cancel** (Esc)
closes the dialog; **From File…** closes it and asks for a `.js` module to
copy into the project instead, or a `.fjgraphic` to import (see
[Sharing a graphic](#sharing-a-graphic)). **Export…**, at the far left, saves the chosen
graphic to share (see [Sharing a graphic](#sharing-a-graphic)).

A module of your own goes into a category by giving its `meta` a `category`
(and a `description` for the line under the preview); one without a category
is listed under **Other**, last (see the [graphics reference](../graphics-api.md)).

Inserting a template:

1. Copies the module into the project's `graphics/` folder under a free name
   (a second Lower third becomes `lower-third-2`, and so on). The two then
   show under This Project as "Lower third — lower-third" and "Lower third —
   lower-third-2".
2. Places one graphic clip at the playhead, on the front track if it fits
   there, otherwise on a new track above everything. With a nest open, the
   clip goes on the nest's front track, or a new track inside the nest.
3. Selects the new clip so the inspector shows its Graphic sub-tab.

Inserting a graphic from **This Project** places a clip drawn by that module
as it is, the same way, and copies nothing.

**From File…** names the module after the chosen file: the name is
lowercased, each run of characters other than a–z and 0–9 becomes one `-`,
dashes are trimmed from the ends, the result is cut to 60 characters, and an
empty result becomes `graphic` (so `My Title.js` becomes `my-title`). If that
name is taken, it gets `-2`, `-3` and so on.

On the timeline a graphic clip is labelled **Graphic**, with a `{}` glyph, and
has no filmstrip.

The clip's length and size come from the module's own `meta`
(`durationInFrames`, `width`, `height`) when it gives them; otherwise it is
5 seconds long and the canvas's size. A graphic is placed at Fit scale, like a
shape.

Placing the clip is one undo step, **Insert Graphic**. Copying the file into
the project is not undone. If the module doesn't compile, no clip is placed:
the dialog stays open with the first error and its line under the lists (for
From File…, an alert says it); a template's copy stays in `graphics/`. A file
that isn't UTF-8 text is refused.

Insert ▸ Graphic… is greyed until the project's window is open.

*Agents:* `list_graphics` lists what the dialog shows, and `insert_graphic`
(`name`, `from`: `template` or `project`) is its Insert; or `write_graphic`
then `add_graphic_clip` (`track`, `at`, `name`, and optionally `duration`,
`width`, `height`, `props`).

### Sharing a graphic

**Export…** in the Graphic dialog saves the chosen graphic as a
`.fjgraphic` file (Finder calls it a Frame Job Graphic): a zip holding a
`manifest.json`, the module, and the project fonts and pictures it uses. It
is enabled when the chosen graphic compiles. A save panel slides down over
the dialog, named after the module; the dialog stays open, and the line under
the lists says "Exporting <title>…", then "Exported <title> to <file>: …"
with the files it holds, or why it could not. Saving over a file replaces it.
Exporting changes nothing in the project and is not an undo step.

To find which fonts and pictures belong in the package, Frame Job draws the
graphic: every frame (up to 900; a longer graphic has 900 frames spread over
it) with its default properties, then each choice of each `enum` property
and the other value of each `boolean` property, one at a time, over 30
frames each (at most 32 of these). A font is packed when the graphic drew or
measured text with it, or fell back to it for a character its own font
lacks; a picture when an `asset(name)` drew it. The app's own fonts are
never packed, since every copy of Frame Job has them. Text and pictures a
graphic only uses for property values other than the defaults (a different
title, another picture) are not looked for. A frame that fails is skipped.

A file name a zip path cannot hold (a `:` or `\`, a control character, a
leading `.`) is stored under a tidied name (`a:b.ttf` as `a-b.ttf`), and the
manifest keeps the original, so a font is still found by its family and
`asset(name)` still finds its picture.

*Agents:* `export_graphic` (`name`, `from`: `template` or `project`, `path`)
is Export…; it answers the path, the files in the package, the frames drawn
and how many failed. The assistant asks before it runs.

**Importing a graphic.** Double-click a `.fjgraphic` in Finder (or open it
with Open With, drop it on Frame Job's Dock icon, or open it from a browser's
downloads), or choose one with the Graphic dialog's **From File…**. The
package goes into the front project — the one whose window is in front;
with none open, a new untitled project — or, for From File…, the dialog's
own project. If Frame Job was not running it opens first, and the package
waits until any projects it reopens are back.

Frame Job checks the package before it copies anything: a package that is
damaged, compressed, changed after it was written, or written by a newer
Frame Job is refused with a sentence saying why, and nothing is copied. Then
an **Import Graphic** sheet shows the graphic's title and description, the
module's name, and its fonts and pictures. Each file keeps the name the
package gives it. A file the project already has with the same contents is
used as it is ("already here"). A module or font whose name the project
already uses for something else is copied under a new name (the sheet
reads "Module: lower-third-2 (lower-third is taken)", or "as `Inter-2.ttf`"
for a font); a font is found by its family, so its
file name changes nothing. A picture whose name is taken by a different
picture stops the import, because the module asks for its pictures by name:
rename or remove the project's file and import again.

**Import** copies the files into the project's `graphics/` and opens the
Graphic dialog on This Project with the graphic chosen and a line saying
what was added and what was already there. **Cancel** copies nothing.
Importing is not an undo step and does not mark the project as edited; an
untitled project keeps the files when it is first saved. If a copy fails
part-way, what it had copied is removed.

*Agents:* `import_graphic` (`path`) is Import, without the sheet; it answers
the module's name, the fonts and pictures each `written` or `reused`, and
`renamed_from` for anything copied under a new name.

## Showing video inside a graphic

A graphic can't read a video's pixels, but it can shape one. Put the graphic
on the track directly above the video and set that track to a matte with
**Track ▸ Matte**. The video then shows only where the graphic draws (or,
inverted, where it doesn't). See [Canvas and layers](canvas-and-layers.md)
for the matte modes and the
[API reference](../graphics-api.md#video-inside-a-graphic-the-matte) for an
example module.

## Playback, rendering and memory

- **While playing forward**, Frame Job draws upcoming graphic frames on spare
  processor cores ahead of the playhead, and keeps frames it has drawn in
  memory while the window is open, so a stretch you play again comes from
  memory.
- **Background render**: when you leave Frame Job alone, the window you last
  used draws its graphics ahead of the paused playhead, so the next play is
  smooth from the start. A click, a key, an edit, or play, pause or seek in
  any Frame Job window (an agent's edits and playhead moves included) stops
  it at once, and it starts again after the same wait. Moving the pointer
  alone, or working in another app, doesn't stop it. It never runs while a
  window is playing, and it keeps the processor busy while it runs.

  | Setting (Settings ▸ Playback) | What it does | Default |
  |---|---|---|
  | Background render | Turns background drawing on or off | On |
  | Start after … seconds | How long Frame Job must be left alone first, 1–60 | 5 |

  See [Settings](settings.md).
- **Memory**: the drawn frames held ahead and kept use at most a quarter of
  your Mac's memory, and less when memory is short. They are let go when the
  window closes or newer frames replace them.
- **A graphic that fails** (its module is missing, doesn't compile, throws,
  or runs too long) draws a dark red error card with the error's text in
  place of the graphic, in the preview and in stills.
- **Time budget**: each frame has 250 ms to draw in the preview and 2 s in an
  export.
- **HDR projects**: in an HDR (HLG) project, graphics are drawn at HDR
  reference white (203 cd/m²), like titles and shapes, so a white graphic
  matches SDR white rather than reaching into the highlights. See
  [HDR and colour](hdr-and-color.md).

## Exporting

An export draws each graphic as its module stood when the export was queued.
Editing a module while an export runs doesn't change that file. See
[Export](export.md).

- An export that would draw a graphic whose module is missing or doesn't
  compile is not started. The message names each graphic and its first error.
- A graphic that fails partway through stops the export at that frame, names
  the graphic, and writes no file.
- Warnings a graphic gives while drawing don't stop the export. An agent's
  export result lists them as `graphic_warnings`.

## Working with an agent

An agent connected over MCP (see [MCP](mcp.md)) can do the whole job:

1. `graphic_reference`: read the API once. No project needs to be open.
2. `write_graphic {name, source}`: write `graphics/<name>.js`. The answer is
   the compile of that exact text: `ok`, the module's `meta` and `schema`,
   and `diagnostics` with line and column. A module that doesn't compile is an
   answer with `ok: false`, not an error: fix it and write again. Clips
   already drawn by the module redraw at once.
3. `render_graphic {name, frames}`: look at up to 16 frames on a contact sheet
   (a PNG with each frame's number under it) without placing a clip; `frame`
   draws one frame instead (not with `frames`; with neither, frame 0). A frame
   that fails is drawn as its error card, with a sentence giving the engine's
   location. `format: "svg"` answers one frame's SVG text, its diagnostics and
   the `ctx` it was drawn with. It takes `props`, `width`,
   `height`, `max_width` (default 2048), `background` (`transparent`, the
   default, `checker`, or a hex colour) and `path`. A sheet draws at most
   134,217,728 pixels of frames in all.
4. `import_graphic_font {path}` and `import_graphic_asset {path, name?}`: add
   a font or a picture.
5. `add_graphic_clip`: place it. `set_graphic` changes it, and
   `add_action` with `set_action_end` animates it.
6. `render_frame`: check a frame of the timeline.

`get_graphic {name}` reads one module: its source, revision, compile result,
the clips it draws, and `kept`, its kept revisions, newest first.
`get_graphic {}` reads the folder: its path (and whether it exists yet), every
module with its revision, `ok` and clips, the font families and pictures
available, the scan's `warnings`, and `history`, every name with kept
versions, deleted modules included. An agent may also edit the folder with
its own file tools; the app sees the change within a moment.

File writes (`write_graphic`, `restore_graphic`, `delete_graphic` and the
imports) are not undo steps and don't mark the project edited. Placing and
changing clips, and `rename_graphic`'s change to the clips, are undo steps.

## Limits

- A graphic draws at most 8192 pixels on a side.
- Properties show only when all the selected clips share one module, and
  Timeline only for a single clip.
- A clip stores at most 64 property values.
- Rename Graphic… is unavailable while a nest is open.
- Delete Graphic… is refused while any clip, including one inside a nest,
  uses the module.
- Only the last 10 versions of each module are kept.
- Frame Job watches the first 16 module, font and picture files one by one. In
  a folder with more, a save that rewrites a later file in place may not show
  until something else in the folder changes.
- The memory used for drawn frames is capped at a quarter of the Mac's.

# Screen recording

Frame Job records your screen itself. You can record a whole display or a single window, with system audio, your microphone and rings around your clicks, and the recording goes straight into a project. You can also record a camera, on its own or beside the screen as a talking head in the corner, and a voice-over, which is the microphone alone with no picture, at the playhead of the project you're editing. Every recording is an ordinary movie or audio file on disk, and Frame Job imports it the way it imports any other media, so every edit, effect and export works on it.

## Opening the recorder

Choose **File ▸ New Recording…** (⌥⌘N), or click **New Recording…** on the welcome window. A small floating panel titled **New Recording** opens. You don't need a project open.

The panel floats above other windows and doesn't make Frame Job the active app when you click it. That lets you bring the app you want to record to the front and still press Record. It also doesn't hide when you switch to another app. If you open it while Frame Job is in the background, it comes to the front without taking the keyboard, so your typing stays in the app you were using.

In the panel, Return presses **Record** and Esc presses **Close**.

## The panel's controls

| Control | What it does | Default |

| **Include Frame Job windows** | Puts Frame Job's own windows, such as the editor and the preview, into a display recording. When it's off, they're left out of the picture. | Off |

Under Size, a note shows what you'll get for the chosen display, for example `1728×1117 points · 3456×2234 pixels`. For a picked window it reads "the picked window's own size". For Microphone Only it reads "no picture — the microphone alone". For Camera it names the format the camera records at, for example `1760×1328 at 30 fps — the camera's best format` with Format set to Best, `1920×1080 at 30 fps — the chosen format` with a format chosen, or "no camera connected".

The footnote at the bottom left shows where recordings are saved (for example `saved in ~/Movies/Frame Job Recordings`). While a recording runs, it shows the elapsed time instead.

The panel remembers your choices between uses, including the display, microphone, camera, camera format, switches, rate, size and the Include Frame Job windows, Record the camera too and Enhance the microphone when it lands boxes. The camera format is one choice for every camera: a camera that doesn't have the remembered format shows Best. It doesn't remember a picked window, the Camera or Microphone Only source (each lasts for the session only), or Record Into. A display, microphone or camera that is no longer connected falls back to the main display, to Off, or to the default camera. While the panel is up and not recording, the Camera and Microphone lists follow the devices you plug in or take away (a change made during a recording waits for it to end). A camera that's removed falls back to the default camera, and when it comes back it's chosen again with its format. Plugging in or removing a device doesn't change what the panel remembers.

### Record Into

**Record Into** follows whichever project is in front, until you choose a row yourself. After that it keeps your choice for as long as that project stays open. When you press Record, the row freezes, so switching to another window during the recording doesn't change where the recording goes.

## Choosing what to record

### A display

Choose a display by name in **Source**. Frame Job's own windows are left out of a display recording unless **Include Frame Job windows** is on. Even with the box on, the recorder panel itself is never in the picture. The panel leaves the screen as soon as the recording starts.

Frame Job's own sound is never recorded, with or without the box. That means you can play the timeline during a recording and it won't end up in the file.

### A window

Choose **Window…** in **Source** and macOS's window picker opens. Click the window you want. The Source row then reads **Window (picked)** and the recording is that window alone, at its own size. If you cancel the picker, Source goes back to the display you used last. If the picker can't open at all, Source also goes back to the display you used last, and the note reads "The window picker could not open: …" with the reason.

When **Include Frame Job windows** is off, the picker lists none of Frame Job's windows. When it's on, the picker lists them, but never the recorder panel. The box only changes the next time the picker opens. A window you've already picked stays picked.

If you press Record while the row reads **Window…** with nothing picked, the panel says "Choose a window with Window… first, or pick a display." and nothing records.

### A camera

Choose **Camera** in **Source**, then the camera in **Camera**:

- **System Audio**, **Show Clicks**, **Size**, **Include Frame Job windows** and **Rate** grey out. Their values are kept for next time. A camera records at the format chosen in **Format**, at that format's highest frame rate. **Best** is the largest size wider than tall that runs at 30 fps or more. The note under Size names the format.
- **Microphone** and **Record Into** stay live. The microphone you choose, which can be the camera's own when macOS lists it, is recorded to its own file beside the movie. **Off** records the camera alone.
- With no camera connected, Record says "No camera is connected."
- Only the Camera permission (and the Microphone permission, when one is chosen) is checked. Screen Recording isn't needed.

The camera starts as soon as the panel shows **Camera**, and the **Preview** under Format shows its live picture. Because it's already running, it has settled at its frame rate by the time recording begins, and its light stays on while the panel shows **Camera**. Choosing a display or another source (unless **Record the camera too** is ticked there), or closing the panel, turns it off. The preview changes with the camera and format you choose. Instead of the picture it reads "No camera is connected." with no camera, "The preview shows once Frame Job may use the camera." until you've allowed the Camera permission (showing the panel never asks for it, pressing Record does), or the reason the camera couldn't start. Choosing **Camera** again or reopening the panel tries again. **The panel stays up** while a camera records, as it does for a voice-over: nothing on screen is filmed. Its controls lock, the meter stays live, the footnote shows ● or ❚❚ and the elapsed time, Record reads **Stop**, and a **Pause** / **Resume** button appears beside it. If you close the panel, the recording carries on.

The camera's movie lands like a screen recording's picture: on the front track if it fits, else on a new track in front, with the microphone on a new back track named **Microphone**. As a new project, the canvas is the movie's size at the format's frame rate. If the camera stops on its own (for example, it's unplugged), the recording ends there, what was captured lands, and the note gives the reason followed by "What was captured was added." If the camera hadn't settled at its frame rate when recording began, the note says what rate it ran at.

### A camera beside the screen

Choose a display or **Window…** in **Source**, tick **Record the camera too**, then choose the camera in **Camera** and its size and frame rate in **Format**. Frame Job records the screen and the camera at the same time, for a talking head over a screencast:

- **System Audio**, **Show Clicks**, **Size**, **Include Frame Job windows** and **Rate** stay live and apply to the screen. The note under Size describes the screen.
- The camera starts as soon as the box is ticked, and the **Preview** under Format shows its live picture, so it has settled at its frame rate by the time recording begins. Unticking the box, choosing **Microphone Only**, or closing the panel turns it off.
- With no camera connected, Record says "No camera is connected."
- Pressing Record checks the Screen Recording permission, then the Camera permission, then the Microphone permission when one is chosen, then counts down.
- The panel leaves the screen as for any screen recording, and the menu-bar item is its only control.

The recording lands as `record_screen` with `camera` lands it (see [For agents](#for-agents-record_screen)): each stretch's camera movie, named after its screen movie with ` (Camera)` added, goes on one new track named **Camera** in front of everything, in the bottom-right corner, lined up with the screen. If a tool records a camera beside the screen while the panel is up, the panel's **Preview** reads "The camera is recording." until it ends.

### Microphone Only (voice-over)

See [Voice-overs](#voice-overs-microphone-only) below.

## Recording

1. Set up the panel and press **Record**.
2. Frame Job checks the permissions it needs (see [Permissions](#permissions)).
3. A **3, 2, 1** countdown appears in the panel. During the countdown the Record button reads **Cancel**, and the microphone meter already moves so you can check your level. Click **Cancel** or close the panel to stop the countdown. Nothing is recorded.
4. The recording starts and the panel leaves the screen. With **Source** set to **Camera** or **Microphone Only**, the panel stays up instead.

While the recording starts, the button reads **Starting…**. If the recording hasn't started within 20 seconds, the panel says "The recording did not start within 20 s." and goes back to idle. A Stop pressed while the button reads **Starting…** (for example **File ▸ Stop Recording**) abandons the recording, and the note reads "Stopped before the recording began; nothing was recorded."

Only one recording runs at a time. Pressing Record while another recording runs or is paused, including one an agent started, is refused with "A recording is already in progress."

### The menu-bar item

While a recording runs, Frame Job puts an item in the menu bar: a coral **●** and the elapsed time (`m:ss`, or `h:mm:ss` past an hour). Click it for its menu.

| State | Menu bar shows | Menu |
|---|---|---|
| Recording | ● and the running time | **Pause Recording**, **Stop Recording** |
| Paused | ❚❚ and the time, held still | **Resume Recording**, **Stop Recording** |

The item keeps one fixed width, so the other menu-bar items don't shift as the seconds tick. It comes down as soon as the recording stops.

### Pausing and stopping

You can pause, resume and stop from any of these places:

- the menu-bar item's menu
- **File ▸ Pause Recording**, directly under New Recording…, which reads **Resume Recording** while paused and works only while a recording runs (it has no shortcut)
- **File ▸ Stop Recording** (⌥⌘N). While any recording runs, including a paused one, **File ▸ New Recording…** reads **Stop Recording** and stops it.

The welcome window's **New Recording…** button never stops a recording. During a screen recording it only beeps, so use **File ▸ Stop Recording** or the menu-bar item. During a camera recording or a voice-over it shows the panel again.

macOS's own screen-recording indicator in the menu bar can also stop the recording. Frame Job keeps what was captured and adds it.

If you choose **Quit Frame Job** (⌘Q) during a recording, Frame Job doesn't quit. Instead it opens the menu-bar item's menu so you can stop or resume first. For a camera recording or a voice-over, it shows the panel instead.

### Paused recordings are stretches

A pause ends the current file and a resume starts a new one, so a paused recording is several files, one for each stretch between a start or resume and a pause or the stop. Each file is named by the time its stretch began. When the recording lands, the stretches sit end to end on one track, touching, with no transition between them. Each stretch's microphone file goes on the Microphone track, lined up with its own picture.

The paused time is in no file. The elapsed time counts only what was recorded.

## Where it lands

When you stop, the panel's button reads **Stopping…** and then **Adding…** while the files are written and imported.

### Into an open project

The recording goes into the project you chose in **Record Into**, at its playhead, in whatever container is open (inside a nest if you're working in one):

- The picture goes on the front track if it fits there. If not, Frame Job adds a new track in front of everything.
- The microphone goes on a new back track named **Microphone**.
- Everything is one undo step, **Add Recording**. Undo removes the clips and media entries but leaves the files on disk, just as undoing Add Media… does.
- The new clips are selected.

If you're in the middle of a drag in that project when the recording stops, Frame Job waits for the drag to end before adding the recording, for up to 20 seconds. After that it gives up, and the panel names the files, which are on disk either way.

If the project you chose was closed while you were recording, the recording opens as a new project instead, and the panel says so.

### As a new project

With **Record Into** set to **New Project**, the recording opens as a new project. The project is named after the recording's file, for example `Screen Recording 2026-09-10 at 14.03.22`, and that's the name Save offers. The canvas takes the movie's size and the frame rate you chose in **Rate**. The first stretch's picture is the project itself, so it has no undo step. Any later stretches, the microphone and a camera recorded beside the screen are added as one undo step: for a single stretch, **Add Microphone** with a microphone, **Add Camera** with a camera, or **Add Camera and Microphone** with both, and **Add Recording Segments** otherwise. A new project made from a recording is unsaved and asks before it closes.

### Enhancing the microphone

With **Enhance the microphone when it lands** ticked, the recording lands exactly as it would otherwise, and then Frame Job runs [Enhance Voice](audio.md#enhance-voice) on the microphone's clips: each stretch's microphone file, or a voice-over's files. It never touches the picture, a camera or the system audio. Enhance Voice needs the microphone's sound analysed first (its loudness and its speech), which takes a few seconds after the files land; it then runs under the **Measuring Sound** sheet, at Normalize's target loudness, and its settings appear in the clip's Sound tab.

It's its own undo step, **Enhance Voice**, after the landing's. Edit ▸ Undo first reads **Undo Enhance Voice**, which takes the processing off and keeps the recording; in an open project the next undo is **Undo Add Recording**. In a new project the next is the landing's own step (**Add Microphone**, **Add Camera and Microphone** or **Add Recording Segments**), or nothing when the recording is a single file, which is the project itself.

It waits while you drag in the project, while a sheet is up on its window, or while you're inside another nest than the one the recording landed in. Pressing **Cancel** on the Measuring Sound sheet leaves the clips as they landed. When there's nothing to enhance (a silent microphone, for example), or the sound wasn't analysed within 5 minutes, the reason appears at the foot of the inspector, and you can select the clip and choose **Clip ▸ Enhance Voice** yourself.

### When the panel comes back

A recording that lands cleanly doesn't bring the panel back. Press ⌥⌘N to open it again. The panel returns on its own, with a note, only when it was on screen when the recording began and there's something to say, for example:

- the recording was stopped from macOS's indicator, or the display slept or went away, or the camera stopped on its own
- the project you chose had closed, so it opened as a new project
- a stretch's movie couldn't be read (for example an empty file from a pause right after a resume) and was left out. Its microphone file still lands on the Microphone track where the picture would have been, and the next picture starts after that gap. The note names the left-out file and the files it kept. Only a recording with no readable movie at all fails, and its note names every file.
- the files didn't finish writing within 10 s of Stop. The note reads "The recording did not finish writing within 10 s." and names the movie and microphone files kept on disk.
- the microphone stopped or failed (the picture still landed)
- a resume failed
- a file couldn't be placed and was added to the media list only
- the recording was saved but couldn't be added. The note reads "The recording was saved at … but could not be added: …" and names every file.

## Files and formats

Recordings are saved in **`~/Movies/Frame Job Recordings/`**, which Frame Job creates the first time it's needed. They're never stored inside the project package. To carry them into the package, use Consolidate (see [Projects and media](projects-and-media.md)).

| File | Name | Format |
|---|---|---|
| Screen recording | `Screen Recording 2026-09-10 at 14.03.22.mov` | QuickTime movie, HEVC (H.264 where HEVC isn't available), with system audio as one stereo 48 kHz track when System Audio is on |
| Its microphone | `Screen Recording 2026-09-10 at 14.03.22 (Microphone).m4a` | Mono 48 kHz AAC, beside the movie |
| Voice-over | `Voice-over 2026-10-02 at 09.15.04.m4a` | Mono 48 kHz AAC |
| Camera recording | `Camera Recording 2026-10-26 at 17.14.33.mov` | QuickTime movie at the camera's format, HEVC (H.264 where HEVC isn't available), no sound of its own; its microphone file sits beside it as for a screen recording |

When a name is already taken, Frame Job adds ` (2)`, ` (3)` and so on.

The microphone is always a separate file from system audio, so you can set the level of your voice and the computer's sound independently. Frame Job measures how far apart the two files started and places the microphone clip to match, trimming its head if it started first.

### Frame rate

macOS delivers a new frame only when something on screen changes, so a mostly still screen gives a file with a low, uneven frame rate. That rate comes from the file itself and isn't a fault. The **Rate** setting is the most frames per second the file can hold. A new project uses that setting as its frame rate, while the media entry keeps the file's real rate. Where the picture stops changing before the sound ends, the last frame is held to the end of the clip.

## Voice-overs (Microphone Only)

To record narration over your edit, choose **Microphone Only** in **Source**:

- **System Audio**, **Show Clicks**, **Size** and **Include Frame Job windows** grey out. Their values are kept for next time.
- **Rate** stays live, because it sets the rate of a new project. **Microphone** and **Record Into** stay live too.
- You must choose a microphone. With **Off**, Record says "Microphone Only records the microphone alone — choose a microphone first."
- Only the Microphone permission is checked. Screen Recording isn't needed.

The countdown and the menu-bar item work as they do for a screen recording. Unlike a screen recording, **the panel stays up** while a voice-over records. Its controls lock, the meter stays live, the footnote shows ● or ❚❚ and the elapsed time, Record reads **Stop**, and a **Pause** / **Resume** button appears beside it. If you close the panel, the voice-over carries on. Stop it from the menu-bar item or **File ▸ Stop Recording** (⌥⌘N), and use the welcome window's **New Recording…** button to bring the panel back.

Each stretch between pauses is its own `.m4a` file. In an open project, every file lands on a **new back track named Microphone**, end to end from the playhead, as one **Add Recording** undo step. It never goes on an existing track. As a new project, the first file is the project (1920×1080 at the chosen rate) and later files follow it on its one track.
